The agreement has, I believe, important effects and implications. The spirit of co-operation in which it was worked out is encouraging. That spirit enabled agreement on a most complicated matter to be reached quickly, and I am sure this prompt and decisive handling of difficulties will be greatly reassuring to the public, including the financial communities, on both sides of the border.
When I say "handling of difficulties" I do not mean either that the difficulties were all solved or that they were glossed over. I mean that the representatives of the two governments were able to deal with this problem in the spirit of the Hyannis Port meeting of last May, when the communique included this paragraph on balance of payments problems:
The President and the Prime Minister stressed the interest of both countries in the balance of payments between them and with the rest of the world. The Prime Minister drew particular attention to the large United States surplus in the balance of current payments with Canada and noted the importance of allowing for this fact in determining the appropriate policies to be followed by each country. It was agreed that both governments should always deal in a positive and co-operative manner with developments affecting their international trade and payments.
In accordance with that spirit, we on our side fully appreciate the United States government's desire to improve its own balance of payments position. It would not, of course, be appropriate for us to express views about the general policies adopted by the United States for this purpose, but it was clear from the behaviour of financial markets at the end of last week that the proposed interest equalization tax could have unintended and serious effects on Canada.
We accordingly made representations on the subject through diplomatic channels and arranged for representatives of the Canadian government to go to Washington over the week end. We are extremely grateful for the promptness with which the United States government considered the problem. When it was pointed out to them that they had underestimated the effects of their proposed measure on Canada, they promptly joined in seeking to correct the consequences.
The modification of the United States proposal which was announced yesterday does not solve all the problems. The tax is still intended to apply to purchases by Americans

U.S. Tax on International Capital of outstanding Canadian securities. This will pose some continuing problems, and the government of Canada will continue to seek exemption for such transactions.
The two governments readily agreed at the week end, however, that the major and immediate problem arose from the proposed tax on new issues of Canadian securities. The two governments were able to find at once an approach to a solution of this problem.
The United States government has recognized that Canada's case is different from that of other countries in that, while capital moves from the United States to Canada, it thereby only helps to finance the excess of Canadian purchases of goods and services from the United States compared with American purchases from us. In the final result we are suppliers of exchange to the United States, not removers of exchange from the United States. In recognition of this the United States government has recorded its hope and expectation that new Canadian issues can be entirely exempt from the proposed tax. We have stated that we will not use exemption from the tax to give us an advantage by borrowing in the United States aimed at increasing our currency reserves.
The unlimited exemption for Canada is to cover all new security issues by business and all levels of government; under this exception there would be no question of rationing access to the United States capital market.
This modification of the United States proposal is a most helpful result. I should like to follow what the Minister of Finance said yesterday by expressing on behalf of the government and, I am sure, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the house, my appreciation of the co-operative spirit of the United States government and also of the work done in this matter by the governor of the Bank of Canada and by the Departments of Finance and External Affairs.
While the immediate result is most helpful and goes a long way toward removing the immediate difficulties, I must repeat what I said earlier about the underlying problem. The whole incident underlines the importance to both countries, as was recognized at Hyannis Port, of taking constructive, long term action to lessen the problems of the balance of payments. For that reason I am hopeful that, in the same spirit of co-operation as was demonstrated over the week end, we will shortly be able to arrange a fruitful meeting of the joint economic committee of ministers of the Canadian and the United States governments.
From Canada's point of view the objective must be a further substantial reduction of our

current account deficit in the balance of payments. This government has made clear on numerous occasions that the correction of our balance of payments position, with its favourable effects on employment, is a central objective of our economic policies.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly join with the Prime Minister in expressing appreciation to the United States for showing consideration to Canada. The relationship between Canada and the United States has at all times been such in my memory. Indeed, in the days of former president Eisenhower the closeness of that relationship denied the difficulties that subsequently arose.
The Prime Minister speaks in fulsome terms of the Hyannis Port idyll and the ideal agreement arrived at there, but may I add that while the Prime Minister was patted on the head at Hyannis Port by the President, Canada was kicked in the economy. The Prime Minister says that as a result of representations made the difficulties which would have followed the continuance of the policy enunciated by the President have now been alleviated to a greater or lesser degree. This still leaves, as I see it, a veto with the President of the United States with regard to the expansion of Canada's economy, which is something that is not in keeping with the sovereignty of this nation.
I am surprised that following this fine relationship to which the Prime Minister referred the United States saw fit to bring into effect an economic plan which could only hurt Canada and damage this country economically more than any other of the 22 or 23 countries included in the plan. As I see it, there was no reason for the application of this plan to Canada. Our balance of payments position has at all times been favourable to the United States. These other countries to which the plan is being applied are in a different position.
As far as our trading relations are concerned, we recall very well that in 1956, in the palmy days of the former Liberal government, the commodity deficit between the two countries and adverse to Canada was about $760 million. In 1961 and 1962 during our period in office we were able to bring about a favourable balance in this regard. Furthermore, there was a pronounced reduction in the balance of payments problem in general during the days we were in office, and I hope that what took place in 1961 and 1962 will continue in 1963 and in the following years.
Our relations with the United States should have caused that country to give some notice to Canada, and to consult with Canada before

taking this action. When the government now surrounds itself with a halo of self praise, may I suggest that in addition to parliament speaking out firmly and strongly on Friday, the major reason for the change was that the financial people in New York took a strong stand, as did financial interests in our own country.
While it is too early to say that this action will alleviate the results that would have flowed from the plan enunciated by the president, at least it is a step forward. Consultation beforehand, however, would have prevented this action being taken. It is not as though Canada found itself in a position very much better than most minor countries, for the members of the press were fully briefed on Thursday and on Friday morning the government of Canada was told what the action would be. This is not consultation in the true sense of the word.

Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of the Social Credit party may I say that we, in common with all Canadians across the country, are happy with the announcement that has just been made; because certainly the situation that was in prospect for us as we saw it last Thursday and Friday was not a pleasant one, particularly in the light of the many financial problems that we face.
However, I believe there are two observations which arise from this situation which come emphatically to mind. The first is the financial confusion surrounding the general situation relating to government financing both in the United States and in Canada. This comes back to the problem of the balance of payments difficulty, which has been increasingly critical for both countries. Certainly the United States cannot continue with the tremendous deficits that they have had, both in terms of trading dollars and of gold. Neither can we in Canada.
And second, I trust that out of this crisis there will be a realization that the old approaches we are using to meet these problems are inadequate to meet our present needs. Certainly this becomes increasingly evident as we see the turmoil in which we have been since our own balance of payments crisis a year ago, as well as the budget crisis of the past few months. As we look at these financial problems we begin to wonder whether the tail is wagging the dog or the dog is wagging the tail. However, we are glad that this quick action has been taken. I hope it will lead to the conclusion that something more drastic is going to have to be done in the near future if we are to find any permanent solution to these problems.

I suggest to the government that it might well be in the interests of Canada if it could be arranged that financial witnesses from Canada could be called before whatever congressional committee may be studying this matter.
As I said earlier, I can well believe that congress will be convinced of the necessity of the United States taking some drastic action. After all, sir, they cannot very much longer sustain a continued weakening of their net reserve position, which will result in a continued outflow of American dollars. If the channels that lead to Canada are to be kept open, then it may well be that the United States will have to take drastic steps to block the holes which lead to an outflow of American dollars in other directions, which again will cause repercussions that may catch us. In fact the Canadian government may have succeeded in warding off a clip on the jaw only to leave us liable to be sandbagged on the back of the head later.
One of the most useful steps which the Canadian government could take at the present time would be to press for an international monetary conference on the question of international exchange, perhaps on the lines of a royal commission before which the various financial and monetary experts who have voiced their opinions and views on this problem could be summoned. Otherwise we are going to experience continuing exchanges crises in one form or another.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a short statement on the commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. The co-chairmen will be Andre Laurendeau, editor in chief of Le Devoir, Montreal, and Davidson Dunton, president of Carleton University.
Other members of the commission will be Rev. Clement Cormier, president of St. Joseph's University, Moncton, New Brunswick; Mr. Royce Frith, a lawyer in Toronto; Jean Louis Gagnon, a journalist and broadcaster in Montreal; Mrs. Gertrude Laing, a housewife in Calgary; Jean Marchand, general president of the confederation of national trade unions of Quebec; J. B. Rudnyckyj, chairman of the department of Slavic studies at the University of Manitoba; Frank R. Scott, dean of law at McGill University in Montreal, and Paul Wyczynski, director of the French Canadian literature research centre and associate professor of French literature at the University of Ottawa.
The members of the commission, whose names I have just given to the house, cannot, of course, and are not intended to represent every point of view of every group in our country. Nevertheless, through the diversity of their backgrounds and interests and their broad experience, they do represent a varied and important cross section of our people. They are all deeply interested in the subject of this inquiry and are all fluent in our two national languages. They are all aware of the dual cultural and racial basis of our confederation and of the important contribution made by other cultures and traditions.
I am sure the members of the commission will enjoy the support and good will of all members of the house as they examine into a vitally important aspect of our national life and our national development.

The development of Canadian unity and the development of our nation as a whole is something which is a more critical problem than most of us understand or realize at this time. I look forward to seeing this commission expressing the genuine will of the Canadian people toward the Canadian unity and the national purpose of Canada about which we all speak, and which we all feel is imperative to the survival of our nation, yet which so often is very difficult to grasp or to actually put into effect.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the interruption was, but I have always thought that Premier Manning spoke, as it were, for the Social Credit party generally across the country. However, I do not want to bring about any discord in that party which has been so united in the past.

I want to say immediately that we feel the setting up of a royal commission is not an effective way in which to meet the problem that we face. It can only operate as an educational body, and all of us would benefit from that. It can only operate, too, as a postponement of any effective action being taken for several years.
The royal commission will sit, elicit facts and listen to arguments; but in no case, of course, can it determine the results of its recommendations. No action can be taken until there has been agreement between the dominion government and the provincial governments on the question of the amendment of the constitution in order to meet this problem. I know that leading members supporting the government have from time to time come out with the rather doubtful plan of two flags for Canada. That plan will not work as far as the constitution is concerned. There can only be one constitution for Canada, and if changes are to be made to that constitution they will have to be determined on the basis of final agreement between the federal and provincial governments.
We in this party stand where we have always stood throughout the years, for an equal partnership between the founding races and without infringement on the rights of other Canadians. Whatever may be the views on the compact theory, the British North America Act is more than a constitutional and legal document; it is the legal, spiritual and fundamental essence and conscience of the Canadian way of life, and there are sections in it that are ageless and cannot be changed by the people of Canada excepting by unanimity among all the provinces.
I would like to have heard the Prime Minister tell how this commission is supposed to work and how it will operate. We cannot change the constitution, as they do in the United States from time to time by interpretation of the courts. The supreme court of the United States in its interpretations through the years has altered some of the concepts inherent in the ideas and views of the fathers of that country. We had our constitution rewritten by interpretation during the 1880's and 1890's by the privy council. However, that is no longer possible.
As far as this commission is concerned, I am not fully aware of the powers it will have, but it must give consideration to fiscal matters. We believe that the provinces must have a larger share of the total taxes collected in this country than has been the case previously. When we came into office the provinces had a 10 per cent share of corporation income tax under the 1956 agreement. We increased that through parliament by 3 per cent. Finally, in the last agreement that was

These are problems that must be faced. The royal commission will merely discuss; the determination will have to rest upon the federal and provincial parliaments. I have stated the view we take, that there should have been convened a conference of federal and provincial government representatives on the questions of the constitution, biculturalism and bilingualism. At such a meeting there would have been representatives of all the national political parties, and a full and complete study could there have been made and agreement reached, without postponement, as to the means to repatriate the constitution, to carry out immediately the recommendations of the Therrien report and to endeavour to come to agreement on those other kindred matters, by those who alone have the power to bring about such changes. At the same time such a national meeting would give Canadians a forum, with the power to act to round out and restate, if agreed to, Canada's national goals before this nation embarks upon its second century. We endeavoured to bring this about on February 8 when as prime minister I suggested to the various provinces the calling of such a conference, which we still say is necessary for this country. That suggestion was replied to. Five provinces, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and New Brunswick agreed with it. Quebec and Alberta asked that the matter be delayed until after April 8. Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island gave no reply, and British Columbia gave an acknowledgement.
Sir, as far as this royal commission is concerned which the Prime Minister has now announced, we say, first, that it is not sufficiently representative. To be effective it should have strong provincial representation. I feel it would have been the course of sound judgment and statesmanship-and I am asking that this still be done-that the provinces be given an opportunity of representation on this most important royal commission.
Second, the Prime Minister, when speaking in Winnipeg on March 8, as reported in the press, said that all ethnic groups would be included in the proposed study of biculturalism. I feel that the very important ethnic groups in Canada will ask why it is they have no representation. I think, for instance, of those of German and Dutch origin who represent one and a half million of Canada's population. They have no representation. I think as well of the Indian population of our country. They have no representation on a commission which is most important to them.

Mr. Speaker, I regret to have to report to the house a series of marine casualties that occurred late last week in the St. Lawrence river below Quebec. Throughout the period visibility was reduced by fog. Three sets of collisions took place and one ship was sunk with heavy loss of life. Damage to the other ships varied from heavy to minor.
The first collision took place about 10 p.m., Thursday, July 18, near Murray Bay. The vessels involved were the hydrographic survey vessel Cartier of the Department of Mines and Technical surveys and the cargo ship Seven Skies, understood to be of Swedish register. Damage was light; no personal injuries were sustained; both vessels proceeded under their own power.
The second occurred at the entrance to Quebec harbour about 5.45 a.m., Friday, July 19. The Canadian canal-type cargo vessel Calgadoc upbound and the Liberian-registered Bariloche downbound came in contact, with minor damage resulting. Thereupon occurred a further collision involving the Bariloche


and a second upbound ship, the Canadoc, a large Canadian laker. More extensive damage resulted in this case although no personal injuries were suffered. All three ships proceeded to repair berths under their own power.
Shortly before 2 a.m. on Saturday, July 20, the third set of collisions occurred in the vicinity of He aux Coudres. The vessels first involved were the Bermuda registered ore carrier Tritonica, upbound loaded from Havre St. Pierre to Sorel, and the Northern Irish cargo vessel Roonagh Head, downbound. The Tritonica sank immediately. The Roonagh Head suffered extensive damage but anchored nearby and launched boats to pick up survivors from the Tritonica. The Roonagh Head herself suffered no personal casualties. Our latest report indicates that of a crew of 50 and one pilot aboard the Tritonica, there are 17 survivors, 18 known dead and 16 missing. The master was among the survivors but the pilot, Armand Lachance, 62, has not yet been found. It is understood that the ship's company of the Tritonica included four Caucasian officers, the balance being Chinese. I am sure the house will wish to join me in expressing sympathy for the families of the bereaved.
Shortly thereafter the Canadian laker Halifax appeared on the scene and assisted with rescue operations. She was not involved in the collision and suffered no damage or casualties.
About two hours after the sinking the outbound Spanish cargo ship Conde de Fontanar entered the area at slow speed and came into light contact with the superstructure of the sunken vessel. She thereupon picked up over the bow further survivors who were clinging to the funnel of the Tritonica, which protruded above the water. The Halifax continued on her way, the Conde de Fontanar returned under her own power to Quebec for inspection of possible damage, and the Roonagh Head remained at anchor awaiting assistance for the return to Quebec for repairs. The survivors from the Tritonica are now in the veterans military hospital, Ste. Foy.
On the report of this incident being received, Foundation Maritime were advised and dispatched their salvage tug. The Canadian coastguard ship Saurel also sailed to mark the site with the customary wreck marking buoy.
A preliminary investigation in accordance with the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act is being undertaken immediately to report upon the circumstances of the Tritonica sinking, and I fully expect that this will be followed by a formal inquiry also in accordance with the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. Departmental investigations are proceeding with respect to the other collisions. It is

Questions
understood that pilots were aboard all the vessels in collision except the Calgadoc and the Cartier.
The wreck of the Tritonica is in 10 fathoms of water and at this point the channel is some two miles wide. Thus other shipping will not be completely obstructed.

Does the government intend to provide deficiency payments which will protect farmers in seasons of price declines by calculating payments on a quarterly, instead of an annual basis, and, if not, what if any, difficulties prohibit the making of such payments?

The government does not plan to provide deficiency payments under the Agricultural Stabilization Act to farmers on a quarterly instead of an annual basis. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REFUSAL OF INFORMATION RESPECTING RUSSIAN BOMBERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Defence. Since the government has authorized the publication of the estimated number of Russian divisions opposing our forces in Europe, the estimated number of Russian tanks and the estimated number of Russian ocean going submarines, why is it not in the public interest to let parliament and the public know the estimated number of Russian bombers that could reach this continent?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: REFUSAL OF INFORMATION RESPECTING RUSSIAN BOMBERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this matter has been gone into very carefully. As I indicated to the special committee on defence, it was considered that it would not be advisable for the government to confirm or deny specific figures with respect to the threat to North America.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REFUSAL OF INFORMATION RESPECTING RUSSIAN BOMBERS
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of National Defence if it is his intention to discipline the chiefs of the navy and the army who have disclosed information concerning Russian divisions, Russian tanks and Russian ocean going submarines?

maintopic: REFUSAL OF INFORMATION RESPECTING RUSSIAN BOMBERS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. The figures they put forward were given with my knowledge, but in future we will not follow this practice of making public even estimated figures on an unclassified basis.

maintopic: SUGGESTED STUDY OF RUSSIAN METHODS AND TECHNIQUES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: SUGGESTED STUDY OF RUSSIAN METHODS AND TECHNIQUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. In view of the fact that United States Secretary of the Interior Udall sent some of his senior hydro engineers to the Soviet union to study their methods of river basin development, hydro plant construction and the long range transmission of power, does the minister consider it would be advisable

that some of our employees in the water resources branch be provided with a similar opportunity to broaden their knowledge in this field?

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: SUGGESTED STUDY OF RUSSIAN METHODS AND TECHNIQUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having sent me notice of his question. I believe there has been a great deal of reciprocal work done in hydrology and electrical science generally between the western bloc and the eastern bloc, and I think it is probably a good thing if it continues. But if the hon. gentleman wishes to imply that their techniques are superior to those practised on this continent, I would not agree with him. He will recall that less than a year ago we had a visit in British Columbia from a group of Soviet electrical engineers and they were very high in their praise of what they found in Canada.
I can only tell him that if there is merit in this sort of thing we will certainly take it under advisement and try to obtain the opportunity of sending our own men abroad; but I think it is a matter of giving as much as we are getting in these affairs of the world today.

maintopic: SUGGESTED STUDY OF RUSSIAN METHODS AND TECHNIQUES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister of northern affairs whether, in the same vein, he is making any plans to try to get the Quebec water resources engineers back into the fold of co-operative study which Mr. Levesque announced some weeks ago was being ended?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: SUGGESTED STUDY OF RUSSIAN METHODS AND TECHNIQUES
speechtext: I think that with the setting up of the resources ministers council with a secretariat in Montreal we are probably in a much better position to look forward to happier times in respect to the resources in all the provinces.

Resolved,-That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things:
1.	That with respect to new depreciable property of a prescribed class acquired in the period of 24 months commencing June 14, 1963 capital cost allowances be computed on a straight line basis at a prescribed rate not exceeding 50 per cent per annum if the property has been acquired by a taxpayer in a taxation year for a manufacturing or processing business in Canada and the taxpayer is
(a)	an individual who was resident in Canada for a period of not less than 183 days in the year, or
(b)	a corporation that in the year had a degree of Canadian ownership and control:
and for the purposes of this paragraph,
(c)	a corporation has a degree of Canadian ownership and control in a year if the corporation throughout the 60 day period immediately preceding the year (or if the corporation did not have a preceding year, throughout the 60 day period commencing on the first day of the year) complied with the following conditions:
(i)	the corporation was resident in Canada,
(ii)	either
(A)	not less than 25 per cent of its voting shares were beneficially owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada, one or more corporations controlled in Canada or a combination thereof,
or
(B)	the voting shares of the corporation were listed on a recognized stock exchange in Canada and it is established, in prescribed manner, that no one non-resident shareholder owned beneficially, together with any other person associated with him at any time in the period, more than 75 per cent of the voting shares of the corporation, and
(iii)	where the year commences after December 31, 1964, the number of directors of the corporation who were resident in Canada was not less than 25 per cent of the total number of directors of the corporation;
or complied with the conditions specified in clauses (i) and (iii) and was a wholly-owned subsidiary of a corporation that throughout the 60 day period complied with the conditions specified in clauses (i), (ii) and (iii); and

Income Tax Act
(d)	a corporation is controlled in Canada at a particular time if at that time it complies with the following conditions:
(i)	the corporation is resident in Canada, and
(ii)	not less than 51 per cent of its voting shares are beneficially owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada, one or more corporations controlled in Canada or a combination thereof.
2.	That a taxpayer whose business in a prescribed area of Canada has been certified to be a new manufacturing or processing business that commenced commercial operations in the period of 24 months commencing with the date on which any enactment based on this paragraph is assented to be exempt from tax on the income from that business for a period of 36 months from the date certified to be the date of commencement of operations, and that the rate of capital cost allowances for new depreciable property of a prescribed class acquired by the said taxpayer in the said 24 months period for such business be computed on a straight line basis at a prescribed rate not exceeding 50 per cent per annum.
3.	That with effect for 1964 and subsequent taxation years section 40A of the act, which provides for a deduction from the tax otherwise payable by a manufacturing and processing corporation, be repealed.
4.	That with respect to expenses incurred after June 13, 1963 a corporation whose principal business is operating a pipe line for the transmission of oil or natural gas be allowed to deduct in computing income the drilling and exploration expenses, including all general geological and geophysical expenses, incurred by it on or in respect of exploring for petroleum or natural gas in Canada and the prospecting, exploration and development expenses incurred by it in searching for minerals in Canada.

7.	That the 15 per cent rate of tax payable by a non-resident person on dividends paid or credited to him by a person resident in Canada be increased to 20 per cent with respect to dividends paid or credited after December 31, 1964 by a corporation that in its taxation year in which the dividend is paid or credited does not have a degree of Canadian ownership or control within the meaning of pargaraph 1.
8.	That where a corporation resident in Canada that in any year before 1967 was not a corporation that had a degree of Canadian ownership and control, within the meaning of paragraph 1, becomes a corporation that in 1967 has such a degree of Canadian ownership and control, a non-resident person shall be entitled to a refund equal to

(a)	5 per cent of any dividends paid or credited by the corporation to him after June 13, 1963 and before January 1, 1965, in respect of which he has paid a tax of 15 per cent to Canada, and
(b)	10 per cent of any dividends paid or credited by the corporation to him after December 31, 1964 and before January 1, 1967, in respect of which he has paid a tax of 20 per cent to Canada.

That where a corporation (other than a nonresident-owned investment corporation) paid or credited dividends during the period commencing on June 14, 1963 and ending on December 31, 1964 in taxation years in which it did not have a degree of Canadian ownership and control within the meaning of paragraph 1, the amount of which dividends exceeds five fourths of the amount of dividends paid or credited by the corporation during that number of days immediately preceding June 14, 1963 that is equal to the number of days in the period commencing on June 14, 1963 and ending on December 31, 1964 that were included in taxation years in which the corporation did not have such a degree of Canadian ownership and control, the corporation shall, on or before January 31, 1965, pay a special tax equal to 5 per cent of the amount of the excess.

11.	That with respect to income of a non-resident-owned investment corporation earned after December 31, 1964 the present 15 per cent rate of tax be 20 per cent.
12. That any amount paid or credited after June 13, 1963, by a person resident in Canada to a non-resident person, as or on account of a management or administration fee or charge, be subject to the 15 per cent tax on income from Canada of non-resident persons.

the non-resident person be exempt from the 15 per cent rate of tax imposed in respect of such payment.

(a)	for taxation years ending after November,
1963	and before December, 1964 within 5 months from the end of the year, and

(a)	as consideration for the sale or other disposition of any shares of a corporation or of any interest in such shares,
(b)	in consequence of a corporation having
(i)	redeemed or acquired any of its shares or reduced its capital stock or
(ii)	converted any of its shares into shares of another class or into an obligation of the corporation, or

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wonder if paragraph 1 could stand? I will go ahead and make a statement about the next paragraph, tax incentives for new manufacturing and processing businesses in designated areas.

Before the minister leaves the first paragraph there are one or two questions of detail I should like to ask. The hon. gentleman mentioned on Friday, I think, that anyone in a United States partnership opening a business in Canada would come under the provisions of subparagraph (a) as is ordinarily the case and be subject, I suppose, to the requirement of 183 days residence a year. But I am wondering how the provision for residence applies in this case. If a large United States partnership came to open a branch in Canada, would the department be considering the residence of the company or one partner alone, or would both partners live in Canada? Would a partner have to own the 25 per cent of the shares? Just how would it apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I apologize to the hon. member but I do not understand his example. I wonder if he would mind explaining it again.

I am thinking of a United States partnership, a large concern which opens a branch in Canada. This is a private company. Would it have to have a resident partner for 183 days of the year and would this partner be obliged to hold 25 per cent of the stock? How would this operate? I am trying to ascertain the residence requirement in the case of a branch of the United States partnership.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who is this United States corporation in partnership with? I do not have that point clear.
This is a large United States company which is in the form of a partnership.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the United States or here?
In the United States; they open a branch in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A branch in Canada would, I think, be treated in exactly the same way as if the United States partnership in the United States were a corporation in that country.
The 25 per cent shareholding qualification would operate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am still not clear as to the situation the hon. member has in mind.

It could come under subparagraph (b) or (a). The minister mentioned the other day that a partnership would normally be dealt with under subparagraph (a) for tax purposes, but how does the provision for a degree of Canadian ownership come into this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If a United States partnership opened a branch in Canada, then the branch in Canada would be treated, I suspect, as a wholly owned subsidiary. I find I am not the only one who is having difficulty with the hon. member's example. As I understand it, this is a United States partnership in an American corporation and this partnership opens a branch in Canada.
Right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How does this branch qualify? I have suggested that in this case it would rate in the same way as a wholly owned subsidiary in Canada of a United States corporation.
Then 25 per cent ownership would have to be in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right. Obviously one cannot list the shares of a partnership on the exchange.
What about a consortium? What about an arrangement like Wabash mines? Would that come under this provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: "Consortium" is one of those words which I am sure the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings uses more often than I do.
My vocabulary is pure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is one of those imported words. I have never known what a consortium is. I am not too clear about the Wabash iron set-up, but I think we all know that in this particular case a high percentage of the total is controlled in Canada, so it would qualify without question.

speechtext:
Paragraph 2 proposes that new manufacturing and processing businesses in designated areas be exempt from payment of income tax for three years. That part is the same as the provision in respect of new mines and also for accelerated capital cost allowances with regard to certain capital assets. This incentive will be available to individuals and corporations established in designated areas. To claim, businesses will have to get a certificate from the minister of industry certifying that they are new and that they are manufacturing and processing businesses. In order to qualify for the purpose of this concession a business must meet the following tests:
1.	At least 95 per cent of the machinery and equipment used in the business must be owned by the person carrying on the business.
2.	At least 95 per cent of the depreciable property used in the business must be in the designated area.
3.	At least 95 per cent of the depreciable property used in the business other than buildings must have been acquired after June 13, 1963, and this depreciable property must be new; that is, it must not have been used by anyone before its acquisition. This is to avoid somebody setting up a business by buying it from the fellow next door. If there is a newly incorporated company it is not necessary that its business be new in the sense of never having been carried on in the area before.
For example, new manufacturing and processing businesses established in the following ways could qualify. First, a company now operating in a designated area could form a subsidiary company which acquires new assets and carries on in the designated area a manufacturing or processing business that is either the same as or different from the business carried on by its parent company. Second, a company now operating outside the designated area could form a subsidiary which acquires new assets and carries on in the area a manufacturing or processing business that is either the same as or different from the business carried on by its parent company. Third, a company now operating a business either inside or outside the designated area could acquire new assets and establish a new business in the designated area; but in this case, where there is no new incorporation of the new business, the new business must be of a different kind from the other
Income Tax Act
business carried on by the taxpayer. If an unincorporated taxpayer wishes to have a business certified as new it must be a new business different from any other business carried on by him anywhere else. In summary, a new business must be carried on with new depreciable property, and in addition it must be either a new incorporation or a different business from any other business carried on by the taxpayer. The definition of a manufacturing and processing business for purposes of this incentive will be the same as for the incentive described in paragraph 1.
There are three tax concessions proposed for designated areas, and I will be very disappointed if they do not prove to be very productive. First, this paragraph of the resolution proposes that a taxpayer in computing income will exclude the income earned by a certified new manufacturing and processing business during the period of 36 months after it commences operations. In order to qualify, a new business must commence commercial operations during the period of 24 months which commences on the date the legislation based on this resolution is enacted. The date of commencement of commercial operations will be certified by the minister of industry when he certifies a new business.
This paragraph of the resolution also proposes that new property of a prescribed class acquired by a taxpayer for use in a certified new manufacturing or processing business shall be eligible for accelerated capital cost allowances. The kind of property that will qualify is machinery and equipment that would otherwise fall in class 8 of the income tax regulations acquired for use in manufacturing and processing operations. The accelerated capital cost allowances are at the rate of 50 per cent on a straight line basis. In order to qualify for this accelerated write-off the machinery and equipment must be secured in the 24 month period which commences on the date the legislation based on this resolution is enacted. Incidentally, this gives people some time to prepare for this, although I would hope not an unlimited amount of time.
It will not be necessary for a taxpayer to take these accelerated allowances during the first three year tax exemption period. He can take them afterwards, as is the case with new mining properties. They may be deferred and deducted after that period. Unlike the incentive described in paragraph 1 of the resolution, this accelerated capital cost allowance is not confined to individuals resident in Canada or to corporations with a degree of Canadian ownership. It is available to all certified new businesses in a designated area.
I mentioned that there were three incentives. Although it is not a part of the resolution, it was also announced in the budget

Income Tax Act
speech that new buildings acquired by taxpayers in designated areas would qualify for accelerated capital cost allowances at the rate of 20 per cent on a straight line basis. This straight line rate of 20 per cent compares with a normal rate on a diminishing balance basis of 5 per cent for most buildings and 10 per cent for buildings of frame or similar construction. As with the other incentives for designated areas, this right to accelerated allowances will not be confined to individuals resident in Canada or to companies with a degree of Canadian ownership, but will apply to all new buildings in the designated area.
I should perhaps add that this incentive is not part of the resolution because this is entirely a matter for regulations, and requires no amendment to the act. The accelerated capital cost allowance for new businesses is mentioned in the resolution because it is confined to a particular class of taxpayer to be described in the act.
I think those are the main points in connection with paragraph 2 which I thought I should bring to the attention of members of the committee. I will be glad to try to answer any questions that have occurred to anybody.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two points about which I should like to inquire. I think this section operates somewhat differently from the other sections providing incentives, in that it comes into effect after the legislation has been approved by parliament. Usually matters of this kind come into effect when they have been brought down in the budget speech. I was wondering whether there was any particular reason that the clause is phrased in this way. I suppose it might very easily be that some companies might have started operations before the budget came down and they might catch a windfall. However, we do not know what the program of parliament may be. It may be some considerable time before this particular resolution is implemented, if it is implemented, and in the meantime other companies which might be commencing operations would not be entitled to this incentive. Although, as I said, it will probably be in the nature of a windfall, yet there are quite a few windfalls in this which are inevitable, as the minister knows, and I think this is a departure from the usual practice in income tax legislation generally.
The other comment I would make is that I agree with the minister and hope that this provision will be as helpful in developing the economy in these areas as the minister suggested. I think that his announcement today-I did not catch it on Friday until he explained it to me-that the depreciation can be carried forward and does not have to be

taken within the period will tend toward that end, because obviously companies will not be taking the depreciation until such time as it is to their advantage to do so. They will have some latitude in this regard which will be of help. If they are not making money, of course, they cannot write it off anyway; but if they are not making a great deal of money they will wait until such time as it will be most helpful to them to write it off.
I am not at all certain what degree of incentive help is going to result from the three year tax holiday. I know we have a similar provision in the case of mines. It has been a matter of controversy and discussion between officials and individuals for a long while, as to just what benefits flow from that, but it might be helpful and undoubtedly would be to a small corporation starting business in a certain area. But it would appear to me that any corporation of any dimension, any corporation which is really going to make a substantial contribution to a community, an area, a province, is not going to be induced to commence operations simply because it is going to get a tax holiday for the first three years.
I can think of some that have started in Nova Scotia within the last few months. One or two of them are million dollar corporations. I am quite sure they would not have been influenced by the fact that they might or might not get a tax holiday for that period of time. As a matter of fact, they probably do not intend to make a profit during the first few years because the period of organization is a difficult one. The minister knows better than most of us the difficulties that confront them. Therefore I simply suggest that I hope his optimism is justified. I doubt very much that it is in that particular case, although I think it would be with other incentives.

Before the minister replies, I have a related question to the first one put by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. Would it be that this phrase "effective date" with respect to paragraph 2 of this resolution, indicating the enactment of the legislation, is related to the provision in the department of industry bill which creates the area development council, and which legislation comes into effect on proclamation rather than the other date? Therefore, you could not get a designated area until the department of industry bill becomes effective?

There is one point I wanted to mention and on which I should like some further clarification. It concerns this provision for a prescribed area in Canada. Does this mean an area of business, or is it confined to a geographical area? If it is a geographical area to which the minister is referring, what

are the qualifications to establish a prescribed area? For example, how large must an area be? Must there be a certain degree, even though it is difficult to measure, of economic stagnation, if you want to call it that? Would the unemployment level in this area be a factor in determining it?
I think perhaps if the minister would give us a little bit more clarification concerning the qualifications for setting up a prescribed area, that may answer many of the questions I have. Perhaps if the situation is not clear then, I could ask him some more questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I should start answering a few of these questions before there are too many of them. The first question was, why wait for the enactment? I think one of the main reasons is that this is a complicated enough resolution because it covers a great many things. I am not just thinking of this paragraph, I am thinking of the whole resolution. It will be followed by a bill which will certainly call for pretty careful study by parliament before it is enacted. I would think it would be unwise for taxpayers to take advantage of this particular proposal until they see clearly in the bill just who is going to qualify and who is not.
The other point, of course, is that the designated areas had not yet been determined when this resolution was drawn. The department of industry bill had not been passed. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings mentioned Nova Scotia in a way which led me to think he assumed Nova Scotia would be included as a designated area.
Perhaps in part.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Only in part, then perhaps- no, I will not go into that. I am not yet able to answer your question as to the definition of designated areas, because those will be determined after the department of industry has had a chance to consider the matter with the Department of Labour and the other departments concerned. Certainly, it will be based on geography, and the factors that will be taken into account are the question of economic development in the area, the question of the level of unemployment in the area, and so on. I would hope that the areas would not be too small. They should be substantial areas or else we will get into a great deal of trouble.
The point of this is to induce or persuade new enterprises to locate in the areas where they are needed most. I think it was suggested that this incentive may not be effective. This, of course, is a matter of opinion. There is no way of proving it. I have said before that, in my own personal view, this
Income Tax Act
is probably the greatest inducement that could be given to business enterprises to locate in areas where new businesses are needed most. I hope very much that this will be a sufficient inducement to persuade a number of new enterprises to locate in the Atlantic area, for example. I am not suggesting the Atlantic area is the only one that needs this sort of thing, but it is the one that has been mentioned. I would hope this would be the deciding factor that would enable a number of corporations to establish subsidiaries or branch establishments in that area and, in that way, we could begin to make an effective attack on what is becoming, in some parts of the Atlantic provinces, chronic unemployment.
Now, there is no use trying to persuade ourselves that we can keep obsolescent industries in being indefinitely. Some of them, obviously, are less effective in providing employment now than they were 20 years ago. What is needed is to induce new industries to move in there in their place. The purpose of this paragraph is to do just that. As I say, I cannot promise it will be effective, but I hope that it will.

I am willing to accept the minister's statement that he cannot give a definition at this point of the qualifications for a prescribed area. However, I believe it would be useful to those people who are considering establishing new industries to give, as quickly as possible, what the qualifications will be, based on the many factors that will be taken in account when these prescribed areas are named. Certainly, we are not going to have industries of any magnitude set up within a few weeks or a few months after the government's intention is known.
I am a little disturbed, however, about one or two of the qualifications the minister did mention. He talked about the tests that would be applied before one could take advantage of the provision. One test was that 95 per cent of the machinery must be owned by the new corporation. Second, 95 per cent of it must be located in the area and, third, 95 per cent of it must have been acquired since June, 1963. There may have been other qualifications that he mentioned.
I think if we are going to give Canada a service, we have to be thinking more in terms of setting up industries that will have some continuity to them. In other words, if these prescribed areas constitute a sufficient inducement to attract industries, for reasons of a tax holiday and accelerated depreciation, that are not adapted to that area and do not carry on after these advantages have been used up, we would not be doing the Canadian economy a favour, or the people who had temporary

Income Tax Act
employment there. In fact we would find ourselves in the position of having to deal with unemployed people who had been drawn into the area because of this provision here.
When we see, for example, that 95 per cent of the machinery must be acquired since June, 1963, and it must be a type of industry that has never previously been carried on in the area, we must agree that we are precluding industries that have not modernized to keep in pace with the cost of production factor, and which could carry on if they were enabled to modernize. This is something at which we should take a long look.
Next, what are we going to do about businesses that have been shut down and which would be able to re-establish themselves by means of refinancing? Such industries would be beneficial to an area and would have a reasonably good chance of carrying on after the advantages given here have been used up.
There is one case which is specifically interesting to me, as it happens to be in my constituency. It concerns a processing plant which became involved in litigation. All of the machinery is new and the plant itself is new; but because of the litigation their sales contracts became no longer valid, or at least the people involved in them were subject to litigation because of patent rights.
The machinery has been sitting there since long before June, 1963, but the plant has not been operating. Now, it might be a little difficult to have the area in which it is located designated to come within the ambit of these incentives, as I do not think its unemployment level is particularly high. However this is a processing plant that is particularly adapted to the area and which could make a tremendous contribution to its economy. There is no similar plant anywhere near it and I am wondering if it could possibly be included to take the benefit of these advantages.
The fact is that if some advantage is not given to it, the plant will not be operating and will not be producing any income tax. Therefore I think this is an opportunity to use some discretionary power, which would be a little wider than what is proposed, to enable industries to become established, industries that will increase local employment and which will not later on have their employees become a burden on the government because they were mislocated as a result of the inducements outlined in this resolution.

Could the minister tell us whether this provision would apply to a factory where a change in operation takes place and an entirely new product is manufactured? Say, for example, there is a com-

pany manufacturing automobile components; it is sold to some other concern, and then they start the manufacture of electronic equipment. Would the provisions apply in a case like that, and if they apply in a case like that where a sale has taken place, would they apply if the same company merely changed its operation and went into a different type of manufacturing, new to the area?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I presume that the new company would have to acquire new assets. In fact I am not clear how you can shift from producing automobile parts to electronic equipment without, for all practical purposes, being in a new business. If it is a new business under these definitions, then it would qualify if it were in a designated area. If it were not a new business and were not in a designated area, then it would not qualify.

If there were not a sale to another corporation and the same company switched its operation into a new type of manufacturing, which would involve the buying of new machinery, although it would use the same factory plant and administrative offices, would it qualify then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The fact of the sale would not make any difference if it had not changed its nature and became a new business. The sale itself has no bearing on this proposal, and perhaps I might just add a word in a more general vein.
I think members of the committee are aware of the success that has been met in the United Kingdom and several European countries in re-establishing and reviving depressed areas. Now, we do not call them depressed areas in Canada. We call them designated areas, which is a more polite term, although pretty much the same. They are areas where high levels of unemployment have persisted year after year. How does one go about doing anything about that?
The temporary measures are fairly obvious. You try to spend more money on social capital projects of one kind or another, but if you are going to get at the root of the problem it seems to me you have to introduce new businesses into those areas, or alternatively the people are going to get fed up and move away. You can argue from the standpoint of economic theory, and so on, that it is better for people to move away, and that the more mobility there is in the country the better it is. But I suggest that when this happens we lose the investment that has been made in existing towns, cities and villages, which implies houses, schools and everything else, and apart from that people do not want to move away. Therefore, if there is anything we can do to introduce new industries into such areas

it is surely a good thing. Otherwise everybody will end up in either Montreal, Toronto or Calgary.

We realize that this provision deals with a specific economic ill, and that we are talking about areas which have been less developed than others. However there is one problem of a rather technical nature that I wish to raise. It has to do with paragraph 1 of the resolution as well, and is a matter to which I referred late on Friday afternoon. We need a definite definition of acquisition of property. We have to get some degree of exactness of what the legislation will mean by the acquisition of property within the prescribed periods.
We realize that one can take outright title and become outright owner; but does the acquisition of property envision, in those provinces outside Quebec, the acquisition of plant by way of agreement for sale, or conditional sale agreement, which may extend in the case of these special areas beyond the three years of non-profit? It may go on for four or five years, during which term payment will be made. We know that under the provisions of conditional sales contracts, title and ownership to property shall remain vested in the vendor. If it is stated that it is on the acquisition of property, with emphasis on the word "property" in its legal sense, then the effect of such a transaction will be a negation by the legislation, or vice versa.
There is another point I should like the minister to clarify. I refer to a method that is becoming more and more popular these days, which is the lease back. How will a lease back, if it will qualify at all, qualify under these provisions? There must be an inducement for investment in a new industry of the plant, the machinery. We know that there are lease back arrangements which could be used, by the terms of which lease, an accelerated lease payment during the initial years which would be comparable to the rate of depreciation that is permitted under this particular, shall we say, incentive. In any event, perhaps the minister could at this stage advise the committee what the thinking of the ministry is in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could just add one other question to that, so that the minister could have it in mind. I am not sure that he wants to answer it now, but I think it might be a good thing for him to have in mind when the regulations are drafted. In this matter of acquisition there are problems which might arise. I am thinking particularly, again, of my own province and Industrial Estates, a crown corporation, which on more than one occasion has purchased 28902-5-157
Income Tax Act
machinery and equipment for a new entrepreneur and, something along the line suggested by my hon. friend from Edmonton West, there might be a lease back. I think the minister and his officials should take a very careful look at that situation in permitting a write-off, because there are various types of purchases that I know have been made. They have been very successful in some cases. There were 11 new corporations in Nova Scotia this calendar year. I would think it might be advisable to check with the officials of some of the provincial crown corporations which are in that business before definitive regulations are drafted in that particular area.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I could take these three questions in order. When the hon. member for Edmonton West asked me about this on Friday just at the end of the day, I understood his question to be whether, to qualify for the increased allowance under paragraph 1, a taxpayer had to have the new assets delivered and installed within the 24 month period commencing June 14, 1963, or whether it was only necessary for him to enter into a binding contract within that period.
My answer on Friday was to the effect that the important thing was whether he had acquired title to the property in the 24 months. That was the point we were discussing when we adjourned. My hon. friend is now asking if this means, in the case of a conditional sales agreement under which title may not pass until after June 14, 1965, that the purchaser would not be entitled to the capital cost allowance at the 50 per cent rate. Is that, roughly, what the hon. member is asking?
This is it. We are caught in the legal definition at this point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that in these circumstances the purchaser is usually considered by the taxation department to have acquired an ownership interest in the property when he takes possession of it. That is usually the way, as I understand it, the tax department rules for these purposes. If that occurred in the 24 month period, he would be entitled to the 50 per cent write-off. I think the hon. member will have to ask his colleague over here, who used to administer the tax department, whether I am right or wrong; but that is what I am informed as to the way it has been done.

I agree; but if I may interrupt here, Mr. Chairman, I think there is a problem in the case where you have a contract for delivery, where you have a fully

Income Tax Act
binding contract entered into between a proposed taxpayer and a supplier for the provision of machinery, which cannot be delivered at once. The minister said this provision applied when a person took possession. Possession connotes delivery; yet a taxpayer would be committed under a binding contract although he had not accepted delivery. That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that case, Mr. Chairman, I am informed that the tax department would not give him the depreciation. They will not let him depreciate the machine until it is a machine. The same applies to these lease back deals. I think the suggestion that there may be something special in the case that was mentioned, Industrial Estates, which have been doing a useful job in Nova Scotia-
I think there are others in other provinces, but I am not sure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will certainly ask that this matter be looked into. But I think we also have to remember that you cannot get a write-off unless you have bought something. You cannot get a write-off if you have leased something that you are going to pay for over 25 years; you get that write-off when you pay your money. That probably is the distinction. I do not see how you can get any faster depreciation on a lease deal until you pay up.
In the Industrial Estates situation, if Industrial Estates supply machines to a business and the business does not have to pay for them, the only person that we could, presumably, allow the capital costs allowance to would be Industrial Estates, and it would not do them much good. The purpose of this, of course, is to add another incentive separate and distinct from the kind that the Industrial Estates people can give to new industry to locate in these areas. The form of the incentive is reasonably clear, to the extent that it means new construction and to the extent that it means the purchase of new equipment in Canada that will provide work in the plants which produce the equipment, quite apart from the area that is under consideration.

I have a further point with respect to plant, Mr. Chairman. What is the critical date there? Must it be the completion of the plant, the complete erection and occupancy, or is there to be recognized a form of commitment between the taxpayer and the contractor under which the plant is being erected and will be occupied, say six months after the critical date? This is the point, because as we know there are various forms of building contracts whereby the property in the building materials passes to the owner on delivery to the site; and there are other 
situations in the province of Quebec where this may not apply, where they have the doctrine of revendication which does not apply in the common law provinces. I admit these are rather complicated problems, but I would like some clarification of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are complicated in a sense. The Department of National Revenue has established a series of rules and regulations over the years that are generally pretty well known to the taxpayers. In the case of a factory building, if that is referred to as plant, to the extent the factory building is completed, or the portion of it that is completed and paid for and recorded on the books, the taxpayer would be entitled to these write-offs. But he would not be entitled to a write-off on a commitment of a contractor to finish the plant over the next two or three years. That is there now. You could not have a separate set of rules to apply to this special incentive that does not apply to, I was going to say life in general, but I mean corporate life in general. These customs or rules or regulations are generally understood by most taxpayers, and if a taxpayer is anxious to get his new building or new plant recorded on the books within a certain year I presume, if he is ingenious enough, that he can do so up to a point. But he cannot do it merely by entering into a contract with a contractor to build him a plant next year and expect to get a write-off this year.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the incentive the minister is offering for new industry, but it does not appear to me to be large enough to develop any appreciable new industry. First of all the minister suggests that these incentives would be applicable in designated areas, but gives us no knowledge of the designated areas to which he refers. Some mention was made of the maritimes, and no doubt parts of that area would qualify. He said that he hoped the areas would be large enough. Two years ago the previous government brought in double depreciation in similar types of areas and there was a great hue and cry from the then opposition to get the government to name those areas. The opposition of that day said they could not judge the value of this measure unless the government named the areas, and they went to great lengths in promoting that contention. I think we should be given some idea where these designated areas are to be.
Then he suggested that the commencement of a new industry would mean the application to the minister for a certificate of qualification for the 36 months tax free holiday which this measure proposes. To me 36 months is not long enough for an absolutely

new industry commencing operation, when you consider the fact that 95 per cent of the machinery must be bought from June 13 on, and that within a period of 36 months the industry has to get going and produce a taxable income in order to benefit from the tax free holiday. If it has no taxable income in the first two years the 50 per cent writeoff would be of very little value. It may be of some value but not very great.
I think, Mr. Chairman, this proposed legislation would be far more beneficial to companies already established in other parts of Canada which want to establish a subsidiary company, or which are induced to establish a subsidiary company, in a designated area, or what they think would be a designated area. I suggest this would merely mean a different allocation of the working force and not nearly as great an increase of employed persons as would be desired by the minister or the Canadian people generally. I suggest that an absolutely new industry should have a tax free holiday of longer than 36 months and that the 50 per cent write-off should be applied when the industry has established itself and is in a position to pay income tax.
A lot of the measures which will come into force when this bill passes strike a strange theme, it seems to me, because who is to know when the bill will pass? I think the budget resolutions should be approved either on the day the budget is brought down-in fact, most of them are as a rule-or at a later date when the proposals are implemented by the minister, not at the sanction of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would be glad to accept that suggestion, Mr. Chairman.

I should like to see the minister go further than that and allow new industries to go back to the first of the year. If that were done, your machinery date and all the rest of it would have to go back to the same prescribed date in order to make all things equal. This measure will certainly be a big help to industries already established in Canada which wish to start another subsidiary plant in another locality, but I do not think it goes far enough. I do not think the 24-month period or the 36-month period is long enough for an absolutely new industry to finance itself, become operational and start to pay income tax. In most of these areas money lenders are very hesitant about lending money because, perhaps I might say, of the financial worth of such an area or to the risk involved. Therefore they hesitate to lend money for any length of time. It is quite common to spend six or eight months arranging capital to commence a new industry in what might qualify as a 28902-5-1571
Income Tax Act
designated area. One would have to know before going too far whether one would qualify, and perhaps receive not formal approval but a nod from the minister with regard to whether one would get a certificate before actually signing the agreement and borrowing the money. Personally, I should like to see the minister name these designated areas. I think particularly of my own area of the east-central part of Alberta. Perhaps the maritimes would also qualify, as well as many areas in Saskatchewan. I know for a fact that many areas in Quebec would qualify. Various governments have from time to time announced their opinions that industry should be decentralized to quite a large extent. This could bring about a degree of decentralization if the designated areas were so distributed and the incentives great enough. I fear they are not and suggest the minister give consideration to lengthening the period of time and increasing the number of designated areas to as great an extent as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to say that, as I understand it, buildings will be allowed depreciation at 20 per cent on the straight line method, and class 8 at the 50 per cent rate. Various classes of goods must be purchased within 24 months from the date the legislation is passed. Does the exemption apply to 36 months from the inception of the business, that date being set by the minister of industry, in the determination of the date on which the business is considered to have begun operation? I wonder if the minister had any criteria in mind? Does the business start at the time of incorporation? Does it start when the bricks and mortar have been laid, or when the company makes its first sale?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The date would be the date when the company begins its commercial operation.
On the point raised about the designated area I would remind the committee that these areas have to be established by certificates issued by the minister of industry and, of course, the bill to set up the department of industry has not yet been passed. It has been passed by this house but not by the Senate.

Let us say the company was incorporated in the middle of January and they decided that their year should end on December 31. But they do manage to get their building up and begin operations on November 1. Would they be free from income tax for one year, in which they had only been in operation for two months, and then for two years during which they would be in operation for 12 months a year; or would

Income Tax Act
the time be calculated on the basis of two months, 12 months, 12 months and 10 months?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The latter would be the case, 36 months.
There is a question I should like to ask about this tax free holiday, as the minister calls it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was careful not to call it that.

During the term of the last government we set up a criteria by means of which areas capable of qualifying for double depreciation allowances could be designated. Applications came in from a municipality or area and the Department of Labour, together with the national employment service, immediately got to work to ascertain whether that particular area qualified in accordance with the criteria set up. This only applied to areas from which an application was made. It is difficult to see how the government will now be able to designate an area in the absence of a proper survey of all of Canada. Does the government intend to make a nation wide survey of all Canada based on the criteria they have in mind, or which they intend to set up? In other words, does the government intend to designate certain areas without having any means of knowing whether they will be eligible for this type of tax free holiday, or are certain parts of Canada expected to make claim under the criteria in order to be designated. I wonder if the minister would enlighten us on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows the difficulty about doing this because he has had experience of this work himself in the past. I do not want to move into an area for which the minister of industry will be responsible. It will be his responsibility to work this out, together with the Minister of Labour and all others concerned; but I can assure the hon. member that he will take into account all the information that is available. The objective is to encourage new industry into areas where unemployment is high.

There are three questions I should like to put to the minister. In the first place, I should like to ask him what consideration he has given to the re-establishment of businesses which have been shut down. Many such businesses could probably re-open if they had some new equipment and refinancing. In many cases this would seem to provide the most desirable types of industry which could be set up in an area, if only because of the continuity. If the minister intends to provide that in order to get assistance an industry must be one which has

never been carried on in that neighbourhood before there can, of course, be no provision for re-establishing a business which has been shut down.
The second question I should like to ask is this: what is the target date when this scheme will come into being? I ask this so that people who are thinking about establishing an industry can be working toward it and doing some of the preliminary work.
My third question is: how long would the department be prepared to defer or delay the income tax incentive of which the minister spoke. I understood him to say it was not necessary for it to be taken advantage of within the first 36 months.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
First, as to the inquiry about a business which has been shut down. Such a business would qualify if in being set up again it had acquired a lot of new machinery. To the extent of the new machinery it would qualify if it were in a designated area. I cannot be more specific, because I would want to know a lot more about the business. There is nothing in this provision which would provide new capital for a business such as the hon. member mentioned in his example.
When this incentive will become effective will depend upon when the act is passed and proclaimed. I am sure the amendments to the Income Tax Act will be proclaimed immediately after they are passed. Until they are passed, I agree there will be an element of uncertainty because people will not know when they can take advantage of these incentives. There is one other thing:	The
minister of industry will also have to announce the designated areas. He will be planning to do so at the earliest possible date because this will be one of his important responsibilities.
