As to how long a taxpayer can defer taking the higher rates of capital cost allowance, I am informed by the officials of the Department of National Revenue that he could defer them as long as he likes. Naturally, he would want to take them as fast as he can because this would save him money. But if he is losing money there is no reason why he should claim this extra capital cost allowance. If he does not turn his business into a profitable one he will probably never take it.
Did I understand the minister to say in his opening statement that in order to qualify an industry must be a type of industry which had never been carried on in an area before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not mean that to be a general statement. That is not the case at all. I think it did apply though in one particular

Income Tax Act
instance, and I am trying to find it in these notes. It does not apply in general. There is no reason why it should be a new type of industry that is new to the area.
That is the point that was disturbing me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not so.

Did I understand the minister to say that the establishment of a new industry that would qualify would require a new building? I am thinking of an area which I would presume might be a designated area-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I did not mean to give that impression.

To follow up the point raised by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, I should like to ask the minister about depreciation. Can depreciation appear on the books as a loss and be picked up later? I understand the rate of depreciation is going to be 50 per cent. Can it be shown on the books as a loss and then be picked up at a later date under the Income Tax Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not been giving tax advice for quite some time and I should not be doing it now. However, under the regulations, if a company writes off an asset or claims depreciation and writes it off in its books, and makes a loss, it is allowed a five-year tax carry forward of the loss, and it can pick it up in that period and in that period only. But there is no reason why it should write off the capital cost allowance in its books until it wants to and if it does not write it off it can claim it at any time it likes.

I brought up the point because I understand the depreciation is on a straight line basis whereas in my experience with taxation of this type the allowance has been taken on the undepreciated balance each year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As the hon. member knows, depreciation used to be on a straight line basis at one time, but in this case for this particular incentive it will be on a straight line basis and taxpayers can claim it any time they like. There is no obligation for them to write it off quickly, but if they do write it off in their books then they are limited as to the period when they can claim it.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister whether municipalities, that is municipalities in a prescribed area with a high level of unemployment, will be able to apply immediately to the minister of industry in order to get the required approval for this special assistance provided to industries setting up in that area.
For instance, the Saguenay area in particular, which I consider as a whole, where unemployment has been high for several years, would well qualify, it seems to me, to obtain this assistance provided to industries. Therefore, could those municipalities apply immediately to the minister of industry in order to obtain such certification and approval?
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose in a technical sense there is no minister of industry to apply to until the act establishing the department of industry has been passed, but I would not think that should restrain any enterprising municipality that feels it would like to get in on this as fast as possible. While I do not want to issue any invitations on the part of the minister who may become minister of industry, this is a free country and I presume anybody can go and see him who wants to do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Has the committee concluded consideration of paragraph 2?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Paragraph 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This paragraph proposes the repeal of section 40A of the act. Section 40A of the act is the section providing for the tax concession based on increased sales which was introduced following the 1962 budget. The concession was in the form of a deduction from tax otherwise payable if the taxpayer could show that his sales for a year exceeded his sales in a certain base period.
This particular concession was criticized on a number of grounds, first, that since dollar sales were the measure upon which the concession was calculated the emphasis was upon sales volume rather than upon efficiency. Thus taxpayers have an incentive to increase prices or to achieve increased sales in uneconomic ways in order to obtain some forgiveness of tax. I am sure they would not do that but there was that possibility.
That is pretty specious.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. member wants something that is not specious, there was the devaluation of the dollar. He will remember that that took place between the time the incentive was introduced in the budget and the time it was enacted. The result was that many people engaged in export businesses did get certain windfalls they were not expecting in the form of increased prices. If the hon. member for Edmonton West recalls the days when he was Speaker, he will remember there was some discussion about that particular point last fall.

Income Tax Act
Then there are other points. It provided an incentive for taxpayers to arrange to have high sales in one period and low sales in another, or otherwise to switch business from one year to another. Third, it was so complicated that many taxpayers said it was not worth the trouble to try to qualify. I do not know if I can substantiate that, but I have certainly heard it said. Fourth, the value of the incentive was low in the case of many companies. For example, the illustration used in the 1962 income tax bill showed that a company with sales of $1 million which increased its sales by 10 per cent would receive a tax concession of only $1,230, which is not a great deal on sales of $1 million.
Since this provision did not commence until April, 1962, very few companies have yet had one full taxation year under the scheme. Accordingly, there are no statistics available to indicate the amount of revenue given up or the number of companies deriving benefit under this section of the act. As I say, there can be no doubt that this provision afforded windfall benefits to a number of companies but it is doubtful that it provided a real incentive for any expansion or increased employment. It is proposed that it be withdrawn with effect for 1964 and subsequent taxation years.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take the time of the committee in commenting at any length on the dire, funereal record with which the minister has instructed the committee. I simply say in passing that I think almost every budget resolution of every minister is sometimes criticized. I suspect that some of the minister's budget resolutions have been criticized, and the mere fact that this one was criticized does not necessarily impair its effectiveness.
There is no doubt that there was some question as to the degree of incentive contained therein and, as the minister said, the figure set forth in the example perhaps is not one which would encourage a company to tremendous efforts. Nevertheless, I regret that he has seen fit to withdraw this incentive before there has been time for it to be considered on its merits, and I say that because a year has not yet expired. However, this has been a decision of the government and as far as we are concerned I do not see any point in discussing the matter further at this time. I regret that decision has been taken, but its having been taken I am prepared to accept and, subject to what other members may wish to raise, I am willing to move on to the next question.

I should like to say a word or two following what the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has said. The minister

mentioned that one of the reasons for this was sales volume rather than efficiency. I hesitate to put much stock in that particular statement simply because no company is going to operate inefficiently if it means an extra dollar of savings. In so far as switching sales from one year to another is concerned, this always catches up with a company and I believe most companies have found that out over the years. The minister also mentioned that the benefits were so low for most companies, that they were not of much value. I should like to point out that some companies which may have enjoyed benefits under this particular piece of legislation will now enjoy no benefits. They will not benefit from any incentives.
I join, too, with the hon. member who has just spoken in voicing my opinion that the measure has not been given a fair trial. It came into force last year and it is being voided as of the end of 1964. I do not believe the rather vague criticisms which the minister made of section 40A justify its deletion at this time.

I would certainly echo the statement of my colleague from Perth because I feel that, at best, a great deal of the criticism was theoretical and somewhat specious. I would say that the greatest measure of increased sales is the matter of price, and the measure of efficiency is really the quantum of your sales. I regret that this measure which has been given so little trial has been summarily buried, and especially on the basis of so little evidence.
There is a further point I should like to get clarified, and that is the reference to 1964. Is this the taxation year in respect of any company that wishes to qualify under this particular form of incentive? I do suggest to the minister that people will be sorry to see this provision go, because I think you are merely substituting another form of incentive for one that is already on the books.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to repeat myself, and I do not want to go into the criticisms. I expect all hon. members know that this particular incentive was questioned rather seriously at the last meeting of the Canadian tax foundation, not on any political grounds or anything like that, but it was felt by a member of practitioners in this field that it would probably cost more to claim the incentives than it was worth. I do not want to pursue the matter, but that was the feeling of the people who, normally, I suppose would ha'-e been expected to be in favour of it. I do not believe there was enough in it to make it worth while.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does that complete the discussion on paragraph 3?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Then, paragraph 4.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In this paragraph it is proposed that oil and gas pipe line companies be allowed to deduct, in computing income, drilling and exploration expenses they incur in prospecting for oil and gas or minerals, in the manner of the companies in the business of oil, gas or mineral production or exploration, who have for many years been permitted to deduct exploration and drilling expenses. It also permits companies in the business of processing mineral ores or recovering metals or ores or fabricating metals to deduct exploration and drilling expenses of those companies in discovering supplies of oil, gas or mineral ores, since the continuation of their business depends upon the continued existence of supplies of these raw materials. Similarly, a pipe line company depends upon a supply of oil or natural gas, and therefore it should be allowed to deduct the cost of searching for these supplies.

I should like to congratulate the minister, particularly since he is dealing with a subject so dear to the hearts of the members of parliament from Alberta, and the petroleum industry. Perhaps I might just take a moment to read the resolution itself, and then I might ask the minister some questions about its wording. Paragraph 4 reads as follows:
With respect to expenses incurred after June 13, 1963-
This is the date of the budget.
-a corporation whose principal business is operating a pipe line for the transmission of oil or natural gas, be allowed to deduct in computing income the drilling and exploration expenses, including all general geological and geophysical expenses, incurred by it on or in respect of exploring for petroleum or natural gas in Canada-
Of course, it includes also other industries engaged in prospecting and exploration of minerals in Canada. In other words, I suppose what paragraph 4 says in a nutshell is that after June 13, 1963 a corporation whose principal business is operating a pipe line for the transmission of oil or gas, who decides to drill or explore for natural gas, shall be allowed to deduct in computing income the drilling and exploration expenses, including all general geological and geophysical expenses.
The first question that comes to my mind is the hope that the minister will be able to differentiate between what was done last year and what is being done this year. I do not say this in any political way. Before answering these questions, I should like to make a short statement on the industry itself. I suppose this provision is tantamount to a
Income Tax Act
tax incentive to encourage the exploration of natural gas and petroleum by Canadians or Canadian industry. After all, if we accept the minister's word as contained in the budget itself and now in the resolution, that seems to be his ambition. The budget itself, of course, appears to have run into several shipwrecks in that regard.
In so far as natural gas is concerned in Alberta, it was often found when they had what they call a dry hole. Natural gas was not used or expected to be used for a number of years, and in fact was capped in most wells in southern Alberta and northern Alberta. Sometimes it was burnt off as a waste product. It was for this reason the former administration set up the Borden commission. Then, at that time we ascertained that in the province of Alberta we had known or proven reserves of about 23 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. I do not know whether anyone knows, certainly I do not, what a trillion looks like. However, it is a lot of natural gas. I am sure the minister will agree with me that natural gas does come from the province of Alberta.
Hear, hear.

If I may speak seriously for a moment, it was as a result of the Borden commission that the national energy board was established. It was at that time that natural gas was exported from western Canada for the first time. Many people were pressing for this privilege for a number of years, long before the Borden commission was set up. The Borden commission designated the quantity of natural gas that would be needed for home consumption, and the quantity available for export. Of course one could go to the Canada Year Book which showed what our needs were in Canada, amounting to about 10 billion cubic feet per year, and that we had enough reserves for the next 30 years for foreseeable use in Canada. It is a good time to mention this because, coming back to the resolution itself, it has a laudable motive or objective, namely to give incentives to our own citizens to explore for natural gas and petroleum.
This is particularly encouraging because there was a lot of talk in the last few days about Americans controlling our industry. I do not suppose there is any industry which is more greatly controlled by American investment than the oil and petroleum industry. The reason for this is that they have been in that field for so many years and United States companies had the technicians and skill when they came into the province of Alberta. For this reason I say the resolution contains a laudable objective and ambition on the part of the government.

Income Tax Act
Also interesting to note is the "Short Term Energy Forecast 1960-66" study, authorized by the national energy board, which I got today for the purpose of making this speech. Quoting from page 8 it says:
Domestic demand for natural gas is expected to increase at an average annual rate of close to 11 per cent in the period 1960 to 1966-
In other words there is an expected increased demand of 11 per cent for each of those years, and there are three years still to go.
-compared with an average growth rate of 18.6 per cent in the preceding decade (1950-60).
I do not say this in an unkind or political way but I would like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that for many years, in fact right up to the previous provincial election, the Liberal party in Alberta, led by my good friend, Mr. Grant MacEwan, was the party opposed to the export of natural gas in Alberta. However there was pressure brought to bear by myself and all hon. members from Alberta, from 1958 onwards, to make certain that we got cracking on the export of natural gas, not only because of what it means to the economy of the province but because it helps Canada with its imbalance of trade, and in money relations with the United States. This study continues:
Natural gas markets in 1950 were restricted largely to the province of Alberta.
At this point I might say that there has been a tremendous development in the province of Saskatchewan in latter years. That development was delayed because of lack of confidence in the government which came into office in 1944, but since that time more confidence has developed and progress has been made in this field.
The rapid growth in the succeeding decade and in the forecast period can be related to vastly increased supply and the construction of large diameter, long distance transmission lines connecting western Canadian reserves to markets from Vancouver to Montreal.
The next part is very interesting:
Exports of natural gas rose from virtually nothing in 1950 to 110 billion cubic feet in 1960. By 1966 exports are conservatively estimated to be in the 400 billion cubic feet range. For the purpose of this study, it was assumed that no additional federal government licences to export gas would become effective in the next three years and that exports would approach the maximum allowed under licence, except for the interruptible volumes licensed for export at Niagara.
In the period 1960 to 1966 natural gas production is expected to grow at an average rate of 15 per cent per annum, compared with an average of 22 per cent per annum in the previous decade.
Just pausing there, Mr. Chairman, I would point out that there have been many plants built in the province of Alberta. Only last year a new $66 million petro-gas plant was

opened north of Calgary, to handle byproducts from this industry. It is these plants that have made the province of Alberta so economically sound. It is the royalties from the petroleum and natural gas industry that allow the government to develop the province extensively.
I am not going to take anything away from the provincial government in this regard. I could talk for a long time about differences of opinion with regard to oil policies, but I think the provincial government from the outset set about encouraging investment in the province, and one has to give credit where credit is due.
Hear, hear.

I knew this would cause some excitement on my left, but I say this without any reservations whatsoever.
I am very happy to see the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, the former minister of trade and commerce, present in the chamber, because it was under his direction that the Borden commission came out with its report and the national energy board was established. I remember so well, and it seems such a short time ago, when he outlined the objectives and ambitions of the national energy board. We who live in the province of Alberta will always be grateful to him for getting cracking on the export of gas. We at one time went to bed with our coal reserve; we certainly did not want to go to bed with our natural gas reserves. We therefore approved the export of some.
As the minister said in reference to other resolutions, tax matters are very technical. I do not hold myself out as a tax expert in the field, but with reference to paragraph 4 I would like to ask what is the difference between it and the budget resolution passed last session in regard to write-off expenses? I am rather disappointed with paragraph 4 because it says-and here I come to grips with my main argument -
-with respect to expenses incurred after June 13, 1963 a corporation whose principal business is operating a pipe line-
Why cannot a syndicate of farmers in the province of Alberta, or other people with Canadian investments, have this write-off privilege against business expenses if they want to wildcat for oil and natural gas? It is these people whose fathers or grandfathers first started the great petroleum industry on the road in Alberta, at Pincher Creek and other places. They gathered in groups and said, "We will take a gamble; we will put up so many thousands of dollars and dig a well." It was afterwards that the big corporations moved in from the south when they smelt the wealth in the air.

If we are really ambitious and anxious to see Canadians take part in the development of their country, this clause should apply to anyone who honestly explores for petroleum and natural gas. I intend to go into this argument fully, but since I see it is six o'clock I shall stop now.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. May I advise hon. members of the committee that the committee will resume its work at seven o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, just before the short supper recess I was discussing resolution 4 and I was dealing with the resolution in this regard-if I might repeat myself briefly-that in respect of expenses incurred after June 13, 1963 a corporation whose principal business is operating a pipe line will be allowed to charge off certain geological, geophysical and other expenses. I said that certainly the resolution does not apply to all Canadians, to people living in Alberta and outside Alberta who wish to form a syndicate. I commended the minister on his action to have more Canadians invest in their own industry.
I do not suppose, as I said before the supper hour, that any industry is controlled more by outside, foreign investors than is the oil industry. It is only a month or two months ago that one of the last major Canadian oil companies in Alberta sold out to Shell. I was quite complimentary to the minister when I said that behind this measure, as was behind the policy of the previous government when they brought in a similar resolution with reference to these expenses, is the intention to encourage Canadians to invest in their own industry and to invest particularly in the exploration and discovery of natural gas and petroleum.
Before the supper adjournment I was speaking off the cuff when giving figures in reference to the Borden royal commission on energy in 1957. I have since had an opportunity to check these figures. I said there were 27 trillion cubic feet of reserves in Alberta. That should have been 23.3 trillion cubic feet. I pointed out at that time that the Borden commission stated that Canada needed approximately 10 billion cubic feet of natural gas per year for its foreseeable economic demands either domestic or industrial. I pointed out also that we were the only party that has been consistent in reference to the export of natural gas from the 28902-5-158
Income Tax Act
prairie provinces as being not only important to the economy of the west but also to the economy of Canada as a whole, because by the export of natural gas to the United States we would bring about a closer balance of trade relations with the United States and alleviate the imbalance in regard to foreign exchange between our two countries.
I pointed out, also-and I wish to repeat this and put it on record again-that other parties were just as consistent in the opposite philosophy. It was the Liberal provincial party that consistently throughout the years opposed the export of natural gas from the province of Alberta. They opposed it, I suppose, on grounds that they felt were justified in this regard, that we might run out of natural gas for the domestic and industrial use of Canada.
I have also pointed out today that we went to bed with our coal in Alberta. When I first came into the House of Commons, every newly elected Conservative member from the province of Alberta pressed our own government and others for action in the export of natural gas, because when there is a demand for a commodity, that commodity will be produced. When we talk about production of that commodity, then we will really get out and explore for it, irrespective of what the tax incentives may be.
It is rather interesting to put on record once again an article from the December 11, 1957 issue of the Calgary Albertan, which I placed on record on May 25, 1959, when I paid a most deserved compliment to the former minister of trade and commerce, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, the person who finally got the movement of natural gas out of the prairies so we would have a full economy in the west and be able to bring about economic stability not only here in Canada but between the United States and Canada. This is what was said in the Albertan:
Last week end the provincial Liberal party had a meeting ot sorts in Edmonton. Naturally it had to say something about gas. But a more meaningless and cowardly statement it could not have made. The party is still obviously confused, still hopelessly ignorant of the industry and issues.
It called for a "maximum availability of natural gas for domestic and industrial users in the province, having regard to economics involved". Nobody disagrees. Nobody at all. But does the provincial Liberal party realize that the maximum local availability can only be obtained as the result of a vast and thriving export industry.
In other words, when you export a commodity and those people who were exploring and processing that commodity receive revenue from outside the country as well as revenue from industry inside the country, you can use that capital back to explore for that commodity to a greater extent. That is

Income Tax Act
what brought about reserves of 23.3 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in Alberta.
But does the provincial Liberal party realize that the maximum local availability can only be obtained as the result of a vast and thriving export industry.
It called for a provincial gas policy-
They had been calling for that for 30 years:
-which would "encourage the establishment of new industries within the province".
There again, evidence is conclusive that the maximum local industrialization will come through a policy of maximum export. If the Liberal party agrees, why is it beating around the bush?
These are words contained in an editorial in the Albertan, which has never been unfriendly to the Liberal party, as the Secretary of State, who I believe just said something, knows. It is the mouthpiece of the Liberal party in the province of Alberta. They were prodding them on. This article continues:
Finally, it says "any policy of gas export from Alberta shall first take into consideration the present and future interests of the province, and especially the matter of protecting the consumers of Alberta in the matter of costs".

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, could I ask the hon. member a question?
I have only a few minutes. Would you save your question until the end of my discussion.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think it will be relevant then.

It probably will not be, because many of your questions are never relevant to the issue before the house. I want to compare that article with a passage contained in the Canada Year Book. If I were to quote from some of the newspapers favourable to the Conservative party-and I have to admit that in the last year or so they are sometimes hard to find-then it might be said that that was a Conservative viewpoint. But I want to quote from the Canada Year Book. This is a work by people who have made a study of these things, and this is what they said about our policy as far as petroleum and natural gas are concerned- because we brought about a new national policy for petroleum, and I should like to ask the minister whether his government still favour that policy, and will they decide to continue it in the future? It is a policy which has meant much not only to western Canada but to Canada as a whole. When the Conservative government took office in 1957 following the Suez crisis there had been a rise in exports of crude petroleum from the prairies due to the upset in the oil industry in the Near East. With the straightening out of the foreign situation there was a decline in our markets. The former Conservative

government moved into the breach, and this is what the Canada Year Book says about it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What year?

It is 1962. I do not know whether the 1963 edition is out yet, but I hope it comes out soon, as I know the Secretary of State is going to be interested in it. The Canada Year Book says:
As a result of important new developments, 1961 was an exceptionally good year for many segments of the petroleum and natural gas industries. The production and transportation sectors of the petroleum industry benefited greatly from the federal government's national oil policy announced on Feb. 1, which was designed to achieve increased domestic production on a voluntary basis. Approximately one-half of Canada's crude-oil-producing capacity has been shut-in in recent years; the oil policy set production targets for Canadian producers so that a more favourable production-to-consumption ratio would be established.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Was that the George Hees policy?

It may have been. It was certainly the Conservative policy. I know what the Secretary of State is suggesting; he resigned from the former government, but I am not going to get into an argument about that. George Hees was minister of trade and commerce at that time and was putting forward the ideas of the Conservative government; and no one on this side will suggest that during that time he did not do a good job. The Canada Year Book goes on:
Specifically, output goals of crude oil and natural gas liquids were set at 625,000 barrels a day by mid-1961; 640,000 barrels a day for the whole year; and approximately 800,000 barrels a day by the end of 1963.
In other words, when we took office in 1957 the demand was such that we could only get rid of 300,000 barrels a day. Our target was set at 800,000 barrels a day. With our new policy we were able to bring it up to 625,000 barrels a day, and provided the policy is continued and we are able to keep our export arrangements for natural gas and petroleum to the western states of the U.S.A., it will increase. I say that because we made a deal in light of United States interests not only in Venezuela, but other oil-producing countries.
In western Canada we are in a different position. If we can produce 100 barrels a day in one well we are doing pretty well. We are competing against Venezuela which produces 1,000 barrels a day in one well. The cost of production of crude petroleum in western Canada is greater than it is in Venezuela and the near east. This goes to the meat of the resolution, because the idea is to give incentives for greater exploration. But when you have a demand people and corporations will explore the commodity in

demand. The meeting of demand by supply has always been a good Conservative principle.
The Canada Year Book continues:
In Alberta, the large increase in output did not result in a correspondingly large expansion of exploration and development programs during the year since production facilities and oil reserves were more than adequate to meet the increased market demand.
That is exactly what I am saying:
In British Columbia, however, the stimulus of a new pipe line being built to make British Columbia oil available to Vancouver refineries caused a sharp increase in oil development drilling and installation of production facilities. The 1961 value of crude petroleum and natural gas liquids production was $509,834,660 compared with $438,978,707 in I960.
In other words, for two consecutive years the return on petroleum and natural gas production on the part of western Canadian producers increased by $100 million under our national oil policy and because we had developed export markets for natural gas from that area.
Now let us take a look at the natural gas industry. Again, from the Canada Year Book:
The natural gas industry had a highly successful year in 1961, both in terms of production and of capital investment. Production, valued at $63,607,157, amounted to 646,018,204 Mcf., a 24 per cent increase over the 1960 output and an all-time record. Thus, the large annual increases in natural gas production that have prevailed for the past decade continued without slackening, and the year-end completion of the Alberta-Califomia gas pipe line ensures that the rapid expansion of output will continue through 1962.
Reference need only be made to page 496 of the Canada Year Book for 1962 to see that it has been predicted that with this program there will be further explorations and discoveries of petroleum and natural gas which will bring more wealth to the prairies and to Canada, giving us a better chance to balance our economic arrangements with the United States. I should like to ask an important question in discussing this resolution, Mr. Chairman, which is: Is the national oil policy laid down in February 1961 going to continue? This would mean more for production than any other measure we can take. We have only to turn to the northern part of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan for new development, because there is the supply. I am referring to the Athabaska sands. Syndicates and corporations are now willing to spend up to $600 million to develop the Athabaska sands. A recent article which appeared in the Calgary Herald on December 7 stated that a proposed commercial complex which would cost an estimated $356 million would produce 100,000 barrels a day of synthetic crude from the Athabaska tar sands by 28902-5-1581
Income Tax Act
1970. The government should give these syndicates and corporations the chance to make this exploration and development, and to process the by-products thereof.
I come back to section 4 of the resolution, which refers to a corporation whose principal business is operating a pipe line for the transmission of oil or natural gas. In other words, as I understand the resolution it applies only to those corporations operating a pipe line for the transmission of oil or natural gas. Why does it not apply to a group of farmers or businessmen who might wish to form a syndicate? These people would like the opportunity of reducing their tax problems and investing in the industry of this country and in the development of oil and natural gas. Only when there is a really solid incentive will we get the requisite Canadian investment. They are the people who should be mentioned in this paragraph. I am not belittling in any way the corporations engaged in the transmission of petroleum and natural gas, but let us give everyone a chance, whether they be a big corporation such as Shell Oil, Standard Oil of New Jersey, Imperial Oil, or whoever it is. It was not long ago that a group of farmers in the Drum-heller area got together and purchased some leases. They wildcatted. They found crude petroleum. They found natural gas. They then sold that enterprise for $400,000 or $500,000. But more than 50 per cent of the income went from that syndicate to the Department of National Revenue by way of taxation because the Exchequer Court of Canada ruled that this was really not a capital gain.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the question is asked I think I should bring to the attention of the committee the fact that the time of the hon. member who has the floor has expired.
We are in committee; I imagine I can ask him a question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If we have unanimous consent that the hon. member may reply. Is that agreeable?
Agreed.
Does my hon. friend know, of his own knowledge, that these were Canadian citizens, the people who formed this group?
They certainly were. They were born Canadians, most of them in the province of Alberta.

I do not wish to enter upon a full scale discussion of the development of the

Income Tax Act
petroleum and natural gas industry in western Canada or in Alberta in particular. However, the speech to which we have just listened contains so many contradictions not only within itself but on matters of fact that I think it would be well for me to spend a few minutes dealing with some of them.
First of all, the hon. member said the Progressive Conservative party was the only party which had consistently advocated policies which would lead to the expansion of the natural gas industry in Canada. Then, in the course of further remarks, he said-

I know the hon. member would not wish to' misquote me. I said we were the only party which had consistently recommended the exporting of natural gas. I did not make such a reference to the expansion of the industry as is suggested. In fact, I told the minister that this was one method of helping the industry to expand.
I do not see any point of order there.
Well, let us get the facts.

The hon. member also said the building of the trans-Canada pipe line was one of the greatest moves in expanding the natural gas industry in Canada. I waited patiently to hear the hon. member say something about the famous pipe line debate of 1956 and the stand which the Progressive Conservative party took at that time. I was waiting to hear him explain the position his party took then with respect to this pipe line, after saying the Tories were the only people who had consistently advocated the expansion of natural gas through export.
He went on to refer to the Liberal party, particularly in Alberta, as being against the export of gas. I think if the hon. member will turn his memory back to years during which we were talking about the export of natural gas from Alberta he will recall that at that time we were talking about exports from the province, not necessarily about exports from Canada to the United States. Certainly, I agree with him that the establishment of the trans-Canada pipe line was one of the most important developments in expanding those exports. I think it is fair to say that the attitude of the Conservative party, which was in opposition in early 1956, was one of the most obstructive in the history of Canada as far as the export of natural gas is concerned.
I think it is important to remember that the findings of the Borden commission culminated in the establishment of the national energy board, and during the fall of 1957 the then hon. member for Calgary South speaking in this chamber pointed out that there was a need for Canada to study her

energy resources and consider how these resources could best be used to meet the needs of the nation. At that time the then hon. member for Calgary South, pointed to the Alberta gas conservation board as an example for the federal government to follow in establishing the regulations needed to provide for the proper utilization and conservation of our natural resources in this respect. It is also interesting to note that the board was later headed by the man who was then chairman of the Alberta conservation board.
The demand for natural gas and petroleum is certainly increasing on the north American continent. I think there is a greater percentage increase in this field than in the use of any other energy source being used today. In line with this expansion there is a need for more exploration and for greater inducement to prospectors so that our reserves can keep pace with demand. Moreover, as has been pointed out, the export of petroleum and natural gas is one of the most important aspects of our trade with the United States. It earns us United States dollars, and were it not for the contribution of this industry the position in respect to our balance of payments would be much more unfavourable than it is at the present time. So I endorse this resolution to the extent that we do need to provide inducements for exploration because, as the demand increases, we need additional sources of raw material to enable us to keep pace with the need.

Mr. Chairman, this is an interesting amendment. I had thought when I listened to the hon. member for Bow River that he might be working himself up to an amendment of an entirely different character. However, if he had the impulse he managed to suppress it.

We are very reasonable people over here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Actually I must say I was under the impression that the minister was speaking on the amendment but I can read the amendment to the committee. It is moved:
That the income tax resolution be amended by deleting paragraph 4 therefrom and by renumbering the subsequent paragraphs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I was saying, I thought that the hon. member for Bow River, when he was talking so much about various commissions, had overlooked in his reading a study made for another royal commission by the present member for Coast-Capilano who outlined the general policy that apparently the hon. member for Bow River approves.
I quite agree that the oil industry as such has been prosperous. However, I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North will agree with me when I say that the great expansion, the great development expenditures of this industry, occurred some years ago. There has been an increase in production in recent years, but there has not been an increase in development and exploration expenditures. In fact, there has been a falling off. I have not the figures before me, but I think there is no question that this is true.
I hold no particular brief for this particular class of company. But if it is reasonable that companies in the oil industry should be entitled to explore for gas and oil and to write off their expenditures in this connection against their profits from that industry, then it would seem to me reasonable to include in that general category the pipe line companies that are vitally interested in the oil business. If there is not enough gas discovered, then their business will suffer. It seemed to me that it was reasonable that people or companies who were so directly involved and engaged in this industry should be given the same treatment as other people in industry.
Now, that is the purpose of this paragraph of the resolution. You might say that because this is a prosperous industry, that because it has been one of the successful industries in Canada, there may be an argument, one with

which I would not go along, that steps should be taken to depress the industry, that steps should be taken to make it tougher for the oil and gas industry. I would remind hon. members of the committee, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North, that Canada as a whole, quite apart from Alberta, has gained a great deal from the success of the oil and gas industry in recent years. I do not really believe that it would be in the best interests of this country to do things that would depress one of our most successful industries. I would hate to see that done.
This particular provision, in my opinion, is not a very important one. Nevertheless, it will encourage certain companies that are definitely engaged in this industry and which incidentally, with one or two exceptions, are amongst those controlled in this country, to participate in the future development of additional gas and oil supplies in the western part of Canada. I used to have a better grasp of figures perhaps than I do at the moment. However, the hon. member for Bow River made one statement which I am sure he will correct when he has looked at the blues. I think he said that the production or development of natural gas in Alberta had increased from 600,000 trillion cubic feet to 320,000 trillion cubic feet, but I am sure he did not mean that.

I have not looked at the blues, but what I did say if the minister would permit me to interrupt, was that the known or proven reserves were 27 trillion cubic feet and the Borden commission says they are 23 trillion cubic feet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not want to get into a discussion on statistics, which I do not think would be very profitable. However, the fact is that this is one of the industries which it seems to me first of all, we should be encouraging. We should be proud of an industry that has made a real contribution to our balance of payments problem in recent years and which could make a further contribution in that regard. I should not like, therefore, to see us restrict certain companies that are very definitely involved in this industry and which are in a position to make a contribution to the future development of this industry. I should not like to see the house restrict their opportunities.
As I say, I do not consider this one of the more important paragraphs of this resolution. I suppose that this amendment is to the resolution itself, and it proposes that this particular paragraph be deleted. As I say, I do not think it is the most important paragraph in this resolution by any means. On the other hand, I think it is probably a useful incentive to the oil and gas industry and, to that extent,

it seems to me it should be supported. I am afraid, therefore, that on behalf of the government I could not support the amendment that the hon. gentleman has just moved.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has given two reasons why the amendment should be opposed. He first suggests that this concession of allowing pipe line companies to charge their exploration and drilling costs against their income tax is already enjoyed by oil companies. I would remind the minister that last year we opposed this concession being given to the oil companies. The mere fact that the oil companies enjoy this very special privilege is no reason that we should compound that felony by giving the same privilege to the pipe line companies.
The second argument put forward by the minister is that, while these companies are certainly not poor by any stretch of the imagination, this might increase the exploration program and therefore cause a great impetus in the oil and gas industry. 1 would point out that the greatest period of expansion in the oil and gas industry was when they did not have this particular concession. In other words, the concession is not the thing that spurs oil exploration. What spurs oil exploration is when the company knows it has a market for its product. At the present time the oil and gas industry is not using all the reserves it has, but this is through lack of markets rather than through lack of any incentive to explore. I do not believe that giving these companies additional incentives is going to cause a great flurry of exploration and drilling.
When the minister speaks about this as a rather minor matter, I cannot help thinking of the great plea he made for the tax on building materials, that it was very difficult to get revenue and we must all, therefore, bear our share of the load of financing Canada. Surely if we are going to ask people to carry a very heavy burden by virtue of imposing the 4 per cent sales tax on building materials and production machinery, which will be increased later to 8 per cent and afterwards to 11 per cent, and on the other hand if we give some of the richest companies the incentives provided here, that already have large reserves of undistributed profits set aside for drilling and exploration, which work they are not carrying out, it displays a very poor sense of values?
We feel the very least the government could do would be to cancel this concession to the gas pipe line companies, and I would hope it would even take into consideration cancelling it to oil companies as well. If we are going to ask the little people of the country to carry some of the burdens implicit in the
Income Tax Act
minister's objective, then we should not hand out, at the same time, large sums from the public treasury to oil and gas companies.

I would like to make a short reply to my hon. friend from Medicine Hat, if the minister will bear with me. Actually it is relevant in dealing with clause 4. The hon. member was talking about the pipe line debate, and all I want to say is that reading the pipe line debate I have found nowhere that this party is on record as opposed to the building of pipe lines.
We were opposed to the method of financing, and as will be found at page 83 of the 1957 royal commission on pipe lines, one of the first things the commission found out was that there were 55,000 shares given to a man named Tanner, former minister of natural resources in Alberta, at an option of $8 a share. At that time no other Canadian could get an option on those shares. He never had to put up any money. If he had put up the money it would have cost him $444,000, but when he unloaded them on the stock exchange at $34.50 he made a capital gain of approximately $1,457,500, and it was on account of that that we made our objection.
I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that in my opening remarks this afternoon I did compliment the provincial Social Credit government on assisting the development of the petroleum and natural gas industry. I want to repeat that. It has done a good job in this regard. I have not always agreed with everything it did politically, but basically it has done a good job when compared with sister provinces.
Now, I would personally go on record as opposing the amendment. Anything that helps the expansion of industry helps everyone. My hon. friend speaks about giving to the rich, but it must be remembered that corporations pay taxes and are economically responsible, and as they develop, more jobs are created.
I have only to draw an analogy to the coal operation in Alberta. When the coal companies could not sell their commodity there was no more exploration and no more new mines developed. In fact the mines closed and, as is the case in Drumheller, many of the men who lost their jobs are still unemployed today.
When a corporation is given an advantage to develop and explore for either natural gas or petroleum it can expand and give more jobs. In this way the country becomes more economically healthy, and on that basis I would oppose the amendment.
There is one question I want the minister to answer. As the law stands today, and as it would be amended by paragraph 4, does it mean that unless a group of people formed

a company and went into the business of the transmission of oil and gas, they would be denied the privilege of writing this expense off any other business they have? In other words, does this prevent people who want to go into the wildcat business of drilling oil and gas wells? Do they have the same privilege under the law as it now stands and as it would be amended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman probably realizes if he has read the amendment, that the people he refers to do not come under it at all.

Then this means that those corporations already in the business of transmitting oil and natural gas-even if they are foreign corporations and most of them are-will get this advantage, but a group of Canadians forming a syndicate to explore for natural gas, petroleum and other minerals will not be given the privilege under paragraph 4. If this is a budget to encourage Canadians to invest their own money then I say this provision should encompass everyone, and not discriminate one against the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know if the hon. member really intends this, but it is certainly not the intention of the government to create a class of Texas millionaires in Canada, as has happened in the United States. If one takes seriously the proposal of the hon. gentleman, what he means is that anybody who is in the top income brackets, anybody who is paying say 75 per cent or 85 per cent, can explore for natural gas and oil in Canada; and that he would let them do so anywhere they can by gambling 20 per cent of their own money and 80 per cent of the government's money. If they are lucky they make a fortune, and if unlucky they only lose 20 per cent. So far as this government is concerned it is against that kind of discrimination in favour of the rich.

Just carrying on with what the minister has said, I gathered from his remarks that if you operate a pipe line, then you can start in on exploration for oil, gas and other minerals, but how far can a pipe line company go? Is there any geographical limit to it? If there is a pipe line company in Alberta, can it go for minerals in the Northwest Territories or in eastern Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Anywhere in Canada.

Then this would automatically put them in a better position. The first thing to do is get yourself incorporated as a pipe line company and then start work on explorations outside the pipe line business, and you

have a decided advantage over any other type of company in the exploration field. Is that not so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman knows that any company in Canada can explore for gas, oil or minerals in Canada and deduct the expenses from the profits earned in that oil, gas or mineral business.

I rather gathered from the minister's answer to the hon. member for Bow River that a person, group or syndicate who were in the exploration field were not in as good a position as those who had already incorporated as pipe lines. Was that answer given?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Bow River was, I think, talking about a syndicate of farmers, although I suspect what he really had in mind was-
Lawyers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wonder whether he did not have in mind a syndicate of city slickers who are probably very well off, who are probably in the higher income brackets, and who would be put in the same position as similar people in the United States. There is an argument for this, but I do not find the argument very palatable.

May I just add to that little part of the minister's remarks that I think he fails to understand the petroleum and natural gas industry. For a few hundred dollars you can get a lease. That is what these people did in Drumheller. Then they farmed out agreements. They are not in the wealthy class; they are people probably making less than $5,000 a year. They were able to farm out their leases and under these agreements develop their property. It was from that property they made $400,000. I say that if this tax exemption extended to everybody-not the rich, millionaire companies the minister is talking about, but the average guys in Canada-so they could invest their money to develop these resources, the Liberal government would be doing a job for the average Canadian citizen.
Mr. Chairman, I do not know what the difference is between a Texas millionaire and Mr. Frank McMahon-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; I was wondering, if the mover of the motion speaks now, will he not close the debate?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not my understanding.

I do not know what the difference is between a Texas millionaire and somebody like Mr. Frank McMahon. I do not

know how many of the poor people who started this oil boom around Medicine Hat are left in it, because if one looks at the figures he sees that 80 per cent or more of the oil industry is now controlled by United States interests. Nothing which I or anybody in this group has said today or at any other time could be taken to mean that we are opposed to the expansion of the oil industry. But what we certainly expect from this industry, as from any other wealthy industry, is that they pay their fair share of the costs of carrying on the business of Canada.
The minister is proposing taxes, as the leader of this group has mentioned, for the building industry, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare is going to propose a tax of 1 per cent of income on everybody, including people with low incomes, to help pay for the pension plan. But here the minister is proposing that we give further concessions to a part of an industry which has done extremely well in this country. He says we ought to do it for these natural gas and oil transmission companies because we have already done it for the oil companies; but it seems to me that what we ought to be doing is correcting the mistake which we made last time, rather than extending the mistake as the minister is suggesting today.
We see no reason why we ought to be making these concessions to these companies. If the minister is right in saying that there has been a slow-down in exploration, I do not believe for a moment that the slow-down has been because there are not enough incentives. If there is a slow-down, it is because there has been a tremendous expansion of this industry not only in Canada but throughout the world. The Soviet union is expanding into markets which were traditionally held by western European companies and United States companies in western Europe. The United States companies are drawing increasing supplies from the South American countries, I suppose because they are worried about the long range political situation in South America more than they are worried about the political situation in Canada. I do not believe this extension of write-off privileges to pipe line companies will achieve any more exploration, and I think it is completely wrong to be giving concessions to these companies at the same time that we are asking for further sacrifices from people in the lower and middle income groups in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would not have risen on this particular resolution had I not been prompted to do so by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the mover of this amendment, the hon. member for Winnipeg North. I think it ought to be
Income Tax Act
considered, when giving these so-called concessions to the oil and pipe line industry and natural gas industry, that one of the prime motives behind it, and a motive I would have thought the leader of the New Democratic party would have supported, is to put the Canadian oil producer and the Canadian pipe line company on a fair and equitable basis with his United States competitor. It was because of the lack of this type of legislation in the past that the United States companies were permitted to acquire about 85 per cent of the Canadian oil industry, because these so-called Texas millionaires were allowed to write off exploration charges, and so on, as an expense, whereas the Canadian competitor could not do so. Last year when a similar, truncated resolution was presented by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings we criticized that resolution because it tended to protect the status quo. It was only oil producers and exporters that had been established prior to, I think April 10, 1963 who were given the benefit of resolutions 5(b) and 5(c) under the earlier statute.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Under the 1962 statute. We criticized that because it tended to protect the United States companies which were already there; but the basis of the legislation was surely good. What it tried to do, and what this resolution tries to do, is put the Canadian producer and the Canadian manufacturer in the position whereby he can compete with the larger companies in the United States.
How many of our pipe lines are owned by Canadians?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: We are talking now about the total philosophy of this question. If hon. members of the New Democratic party are serious about encouraging Canadian ownership, especially of primary resource industries, then the philosophy behind this resolution should meet with their approval.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words in connection with the amendment. First of all I would like to go on record as saying that it seems to be popular to condemn big business. I do not think it is a matter of popularity. I think we should consider some of the points of big business. Big business is absolutely necessary, the same as large aggregate is necessary when you are pouring concrete; you have to have the fine aggregate and the large. The larger companies we have in Canada today are public companies in which there are shareholders by

Income Tax Act
the thousand. The hon. member for Winnipeg North mentioned Mr. McMahon this evening. I can say to the hon. member that Mr. McMahon eats three meals a day, the same as I do; he wears one suit of clothes at a time; he can drive only one car at a time. This is all he can do. He can only take so much out of life, and I am sure the people working in the industry he has built up are very, very happy to get the pay cheques they are getting.
I do not think we should be so narrow between the horns that we cannot see out of our eyes. I think we should be considering this from the broad base of the benefits that will come to Canada as the result of more exploration in the natural gas and oil industries. I come from a constituency that is thriving today on exploration. These people plow back a great deal of the money that is made. The gas and oil companies, as I understand it, are interlocked; they are bound together. In the fact that they are bound together we find that a great deal of the profits of the oil companies come from imported products; they do not come out of the exploration of gas and oil at all, particularly oil. We import oil in great quantities from other countries, and they certainly make profits on this oil as well as on other oils.
My understanding has been for many, many years that these oil companies have plowed back actually more into Canada than they have taken out of the resources they have explored and brought forth from the ground. Therefore I believe that this paragraph should stand as it is in the text. I believe it is a good paragraph. Furthermore, in connection with the oil and gas industries, particularly the gas industry, this paragraph will encourage pipe line companies to bring about the use of the natural gas, which is an expendable resource, while we are in need of this commodity. We hope nuclear fission will be developed to such an extent that we will be able to use it and eventually it will be cheaper than any of these products we have today. I think we should use these to the fullest extent.
Before I sit down, Mr. Chairman, I should like to suggest the possible extension of the principle of this paragraph. I see that the Minister of Forestry is with us and I should like the Minister of Finance to get his ear and talk to him. In the forest industry I think there is a case in principle with regard to access roads, and this type of thing, which are capitalized. As I understand it, today the forest industry is not allowed any concessions in respect to capitalization and giving over of access roads, which in a sustained yield forest become roads which remain more or less permanent after the operators have gone. Years pass by and these roads are continually used to prevent forest fires and to

reach forest fires caused by lightning, or some other phenomenon. I think there is a principle here which should be looked at very carefully, with the idea of extending some relief in this respect on a long term basis.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?

I have just arrived at the appropriate moment, Mr. Chairman. As one who has opposed this type of taxation since it was first put into effect, I want to take this opportunity of saying that I heartily support the amendment moved by the hon. member in our group. I did attend this committee during the afternoon but I have been away on official business.
I have been reading about this matter, Mr. Chairman, and I have written some notes on it and I do not want them to be wasted. This amendment contradicts the feeble intentions of the Minister of Finance in his attempt to correct the imbalance of payments through his former takeover tax. In my opinion we should recognize that this amendment to the budget resolution will do more to preserve Canadian ownership and prevent United States companies from gradually increasing their capital in an unseen manner than anything else could at the present time. If a United States company operating outside of Canada wants to invest millions in Canada, it first sets up a Canadian-that is, a United States-company. Then it pays its profits into that company. Such profits are free of tax in Canada and so the entire profits can be invested.
This is what is happening with respect to the application of this resolution, as far as taxation is concerned. Big United States corporations that develop new mines, oil fields, etc., actually pay nothing in many cases for this development because our government allows them to deduct all such costs from their profits. They pay no taxation on that money which is invested in development and promotion. Thus a United States company can go on and on forever increasing its ownership of Canada without paying one penny by way of taxes to our country in this respect.
A brand new United States investment company developing resources in Canada can afford to spend huge sums of money for years on end before it starts producing and making cash profits. We had an illustration, Mr. Chairman, not long ago of a company which had developed a mine in this way, after having spent not one cent of its capital in developing the mine. Then because it was going to be affected by flooding, through some action taken by our provincial

government, it turned round and wanted compensation for all the money it had expended. What do you think of that sort of thing, Mr. Chairman? As I said, a brand new United States company can afford to spend huge sums of money before it makes cash profits. When those profits start to pour in they are cancelled by Ottawa by means of the trick of deducting all the earlier expenses. In that way Canada fails to collect taxes on the fabulous profits made in our country by United States investors.
In my opinion this has been one of the most fortunate pieces of legislation for foreign investors to date. United States companies can set up oil and gas wells and pipe lines in Canada and deduct from their profits not only the things that actually wear out in use-the usual depreciation allowance, which is normal with any taxation system- but they can also make deductions of things they have not even started to use, even things they have not yet built. This unique Canadian device was introduced by Ottawa drastically to cut their taxes, although such methods are strictly illegal in the United States itself. There is no such system of taxation in the United States, and I challenge the Minister of Finance to tell us that there is before this amendment is voted on.
As soon as a United States company begins to make good profits in Canada it can split its stock. For example, with the stroke of a pen a company can create millions of new shares of stock and then sell them to the owners of the company for a small fraction of the market price of that stock. Thus the owners might pay $5 for a share of stock worth $25. This device distributes enormous Canadian wealth to United States company owners, and Canada does not collect one penny of taxes from it. This system is always used in applications of this type of resolution in a budget. United States companies that have large operations in the United States can afford to spend millions in Canada on what might be quite risky developments, such as exploring for new oil fields, drilling large prospective mineral deposits-what are generally termed venture investments. In fact, they are sure of their returns before they start. However risky such things are for Canadians, they involve no possible loss of money for United States citizens. They simply use millions which they otherwise would have to hand over to Washington in taxes on their United States profits. If the ventured money brings no valuable discoveries, nothing has been lost since only United States government funds or taxes were spent. If the venture turns out to be profitable, a tremendous profit can be made; and on the basis of the law of averages a tremendous profit
Income Tax Act
is made. These large corporations can undertake this type of development and investment, which is beyond the capacity of any provincial government, because of the worldwide ramifications of these corporations and the application of this kind of legislation.
When United States companies start to develop large Canadian resources they are literally paid for doing this, both by the United States and the Canadian government. First, as they spend millions on mines, oil and gas wells and pipe lines they deduct the amount from their regular United States taxes on their profits made in the U.S.A. So they are actually spending United States government funds on Canadian developments. Second, after their new Canadian operations begin to make a profit, they again deduct all their original investment, this time taking it out of Canadian taxes which could be charged on profits in Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, over and above the profits they make from actual production in Canada these United States companies can increase their wealth to an unlimited degree just by proving that the Canadian resources which they have taken over and which they have been given rights to really do exist. And they know they exist in most cases before development has commenced. For example, an oil lease which at first is worth little as a venture property may climb to hundreds of millions of dollars in value. Such miraculous but real increases in wealth are called capital gains. In all countries with a modern taxation system, including the United States, such capital gains are heavily taxed. But not so in Canada. Here the United States owner is not charged one cent of tax on his capital gains, even if they rise to billions of dollars.
The newest American device is to set up an investment trust in Canada. We had an illustration of that in recent weeks in this house. Such a trust does no real investing or developing itself, but purchases large blocks of stock in Canadian-producing companies. United States owners of the trust, no matter how much profit they make, pay no taxes. They are even permitted to take their profits to buy up more Canadian holdings; and so it goes on and on indefinitely, building a pyramid of Canadian wealth to be owned entirely by the United States because, in essence, of this type of budget resolution, and the failure of any Canadian government to implement a capital gains tax.
I just want to express my views briefly. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee unduly. This wonderful system of regulations which has been worked out by successive Canadian governments, whether

Income Tax Act
Liberal or Conservative, in intimate co-operation with Washington, I am sure, which has been responsible for the selling out of this country, does not apply to Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman suggesting I have been guilty of this.

No, Mr. Chairman, not for a moment. I respect the minister as a man of integrity. This is the subconscious result, almost, of the type of association we have in this respect. The results of budget resolutions such as this, together with the fact that we have no capital gains tax, is the reason why United States corporations or their subsidiaries in Canada own 75 per cent of the oil and gas in the country. Canadians are able to accumulate billions of dollars to spend on defence. Why, then, do not Canadians develop Canada instead of the United States? The present tendency is, to put it simply, assured by such income tax laws as this, and by the great advantage which the United States enjoys over us in this respect.
I was told that years ago the principle behind these resolutions was to ensure expansion, to ensure development. What consideration does a farmer get when he clears an acre of land or irrigates an acre of land in order to improve production in Canada? All he gets, usually, is an increase in the taxes demanded of him by the provincial government. He gets no consideration, although he is usually a man with only a small amount of capital doing something to increase the productive capacity of this country. Why should not a small man in this position get the same consideration as do subsidiaries of United States corporations?
In addition, the people who take advantage of these laws bring their own labour with them, very often, from the United States under false pretences and do Canadian workmen out of employment. I have had some experience of them. In my own riding employees were brought in as landed immigrants. One cannot do anything about that under our present milk and water regulations. I thought I would check up on some of these people, so I asked the police to check their automobile licences. Practically all of them had asked for visitors' licences because they knew they would not be in Canada more than six months. The same attitude prevails with regard to our national employment service. I know the field managers of one of these corporations. They simply ignore our national employment service, and similar agencies. One of them told me: "I don't want anything to do with your little outfit. I want a group of men lined up in front of my office every morning seeking employment." He did employ Canadians for the week or so.

Then he let them off and took on some more. The core of his whole organization consisted of United States citizens who had been brought into Canada as landed immigrants incorrectly and immorally. In my opinion, Canadians do not have the opportunity to develop Canada as they might because of a tax policy which stacks the cards against them. Only United States corporations are paid out of our taxes to take our country away from us.
I give wholehearted support to the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North. I urge the minister to give this question some consideration. Such measures as this, represent, on the whole, a handout to subsidiaries to United States corporations enabling them to finance the development of Canada in their own interest by the use of Canadian money.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I only wish to say a few words to show how complex is this matter of taxation and how the royal commission on taxation is really needed.
A few days ago, Canadian citizens were complaining because the United States wanted to impose a tax on American Investments in Canada and then, a few days later, the complaint is heard that the Canadian government encourages foreign investments in Canada.
Also, the N.D.P. members stated that the development of oil and gas industries, as far as drilling and well-sinking is concerned, does not depend on the reduction allowed in the payment of taxes, but rather on the development of the markets where to sell those products. Well, if the corporations are not interested in drilling, they will not do any, exemption or no exemption. The drilling and well-sinking will not be carried out by corporations that are not interested but by those that are.
It is not difficult to see that the majority of oil companies shares belong to Americans. However, we are in a given context and we must give everybody a chance, not in the development of profits but rather in the development of a new construction which shall be a new asset for the country.
Then, even if we do not like granting certain relief measures to the United States, I think we must vote against this motion.
