speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we go to paragraph 16?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This paragraph of the resolution proposes that where undistributed income of a corporation passes from the corporation into the hands of its shareholders in a way which would otherwise avoid tax, the Minister of National Revenue may direct that it be included in the income of the recipient. It is not intended that this provision should be a permanent fixture in the law. It is hoped that within a short time, perhaps with the help of the findings of the royal commission on taxation, a different method of taxing the distribution of the surpluses of corporations can be devised to make unnecessary this particular measure.
In any event in the administration of this provision it is not intended to apply it to cases where the series of transactions in question had commenced prior to budget night. I think this point was raised early in the debate on the budget. As I remember it there were two objections, one that in the original form it could be interpreted as being retroactive in its application, and this was not intended, and the other point which was raised by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings was that there should be an appeal from the ruling, and this was agreed to and will be provided for in the bill.
But quite apart from that, the hope is that this particular problem of extracting corporate surpluses without the payment of tax by the individuals who receive them will be dealt with in some more suitable fashion following the report of the royal commission on taxation. Perhaps this is being too hopeful, but I am still hopeful that the royal commission might be able to deal with this particular question in time, so that it could be dealt with in the next budget; but it may take a year longer than that.

I would like to ask the minister a question. I note that at the sixteenth conference of the Canadian tax foundation last year, in the forum on undistributed income, chaired by Mr. R. MacKay, he is quoted as saying:
As you may be aware, discussion of possible solutions to our undistributed income problem at the legislative level has been hampered to some extent by the unofficial knowledge that the Minister of Finance was provided with reports on the subject by four practitioners who have been bound to silence.
I am interested in this particular problem, particularly the part that is called surplus stripping or dividend stripping, because I happened to be in Montreal two years ago-

I think it was Montreal-where a very well known accountant by the name of Stike-man gave a paper on the question of ability to pay. He made reference to the number of ways by which what I term sophisticated accountants were able to find loopholes in the act.
Of course he went into whether this was a moral issue, and whether it was tax avoidance or tax evasion, and he gave some illustrations as to how taxation could be avoided and these surpluses stripped. It was quite apparent that this was a subject which the accountants themselves wanted to bring out in the open.
I noticed, even in the relatively small community in the business sense of the lakehead, that several years ago a number of fairly small companies were changing their corporate organization, and a company that would be, say, Blank Ltd. would become Blank 1961 Ltd. I inquired why this was going on and I was told this was the way in which corporations all across the country were, in a sense, distributing the surpluses that had been built up, and doing it through loopholes in the act.
I was sufficiently intrigued to make inquiries, and I put some questions on the order paper last spring. I put them on the order paper some months after Mr. Stikeman had set out pretty clearly the main ways in which surpluses are stripped under the act, and after someone who is an employee or perhaps a business partner of Mr. Stikeman, Mr. P. N. Thorsteinsson, at the 1962 conference went into great detail in setting out the two main ways in which surpluses are stripped.
Now that I know how much the accountants and the department have been involved in this matter, I am rather critical of the kind of answers I was given. My first question was:
What is the definition given by the Department of National Revenue (taxation division) to the procedure known colloquially amongst taxation accountants as "surplus strips"?
The answer was:
There is no specific definition of the term "surplus strips".
There may not be any specific definition of the term "surplus strips" but it is quite obvious that Mr. Stikeman and Mr. Thorsteinsson know there are surplus strips. The answer went on to say:
It is frequently used to refer to any procedures that have been followed for the purpose of transferring surpluses from corporations to their shareholders with a minimum of tax payment.
My second question was:
What estimate does the department make of the number of surplus strips carried out in Canada in

1961 and 1962, and the estimated amount of money saved by the corporate taxpayers from going into the taxation revenue?
The answer was:
The department can make no estimate of the number entered into in 1961 and 1962. Most returns for 1962 have not yet been filed.
And this is the point I want to bring to the minister's attention:
As regards 1961, it is pointed out that usually no income is reported from these transactions, and that the department could not list them without first investigating to determine the facts of each case.
I want the minister to note that, because I was told by someone who has some experience in taxation matters that the scale of surplus strips in the last couple of years has become very high. I have been told that it was estimated as much as $500 million had been distributed. That, of course, was a guess made to me by someone familiar with taxation matters, but it is an indication of what is in one accountant's mind regarding the scale of the stripping.
My third question was:
Has the department considered appealing any surplus strip to the income tax appeal board and beyond in order to determine the legality of such a procedure?
The answer was-and this is what makes me wonder whether this legislation we have here is necessary:
The department will assess, and carry through to appeal if necessary, for all taxes payable under the provisions of the act.
In other words, judging from this answer the department is not particularly concerned.
My last question was:
If so, what sections of the Income Tax Act and its regulations are considered relevant to the matter?
The answer was:
The relevant sections of the Income Tax Act, depending on the various circumstances are sections 6, 8, 16, 21, 22, 27, 28, 67, 68, 81, 82, 851, 105, 105A, 105B, 105C, 108, 137, 138.
In other words it is an awful big chunk of the Income Tax Act.
Out of this discussion of the problem, and the apparent fact that the tax foundation and certain tax accountants have been both concerned and very explicit on the nature of this business, and because of the fact that there has been some indication that four experts have investigated this as a result of a request by the Minister of Finance, I would like to know more from the minister about the temporary nature of this resolution. How will it really work in blocking this up, and is it going to raise or put in question the processes that have been developed-the kind
Income Tax Act
of processes developed by Mr. Stikeman and Mr. Thorsteinsson as outlined in their papers?
If it is going to do this, then the question arises, why would these just be temporary measures? I would like to ask the minister whether he is considering what has been done in the past, that is, making in effect in law some kind of special dispensation at a special dispensation rate, so that you could have these one-shot dispensations of surpluses, say, at the rate of 10 per cent or 15 per cent? If it cannot be done that way-and I would like to know whether the minister has considered it-how does he plan to handle this particular problem of the accumulation of surpluses within corporations and the distaste for distributing them through the shareholders because of the imposition of taxation upon the individual? It seems to me that this is a very real problem. I am interested in it, if I could make a bow to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, because of the point he raised as to the philosophical question that is involved here, which is very intriguing, in the sense that he indicated there was a real philosophy in connection with pipe line companies. I wonder whether the minister could give us more on the philosophy here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to begin by saying that I doubt very much if Mr. Stikeman would like to be referred to as an accountant. He is a distinguished member of the legal profession and is not an accountant. I will not say any more about that. I believe the hon. member at one time enjoyed life as a librarian, and I can assure him that neither the accounting nor the legal profession are very similar to that of a librarian, and they are also very different as distinguished between themselves.
The hon. member referred to a report made to the minister of finance by four experts, and I would like to assure him that they were four experts employed by a former minister of finance. They did make a report on this general subject. I think he referred to the fact that the report was a secret one. I was asked if it might be made available to the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Ontario for them to study. I released it to them and made it public at the time, so there is nothing secret about it.
As to the way to deal with this problem, I think the best answer I can give to that question is that, as the hon. member will appreciate, the budget contained quite a number of provisions designed to plug loopholes. There were a whole lot of them and we will be dealing with them in the succeeding paragraphs of this resolution. One of the big

Income Tax Act
loopholes was this question of dividend stripping. I do not know where the term originated. I am informed that it originated in the United Kingdom, where I believe they go in for that sort of thing to a greater extent than perhaps we do here.
Is that what the members who attended the NATO parliamentarians meeting in Paris saw last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was not on that trip, but I understand from some of those who were that there was none of that sort of thing there. As the hon. member pointed out in quoting Mr. Stikeman and his associates, there are a variety of ways in which surplus funds can be withdrawn from a corporation without attracting tax in the hands of the recipient. There are, as he pointed out, a whole series of sections in the act which in one way or another were designed to stop this. They have proved to be less than successful. It seemed to me that there was no simple answer. I certainly do not know the simple answer to this problem. On the other hand I did not feel that in introducing a series of measures to plug loopholes it would be very realistic unless we did something about this one. So pending the more detailed studies that the royal commission is engaged upon, it seemed to me that the only practical approach for the time being was to suggest to the house that the Minister of National Revenue be given authority to look through these complicated transactions to see if the net result was that money came out of a corporation and into the hands of a shareholder without the payment of tax. I do not like this way of doing things any more than anybody else does, but until we found a solution that will work, I thought it was better for me to recommend to the house that some action be taken, rather than just to let the thing go scot free for another year or another two years.
I have no doubt that the fact the minister will be given power to look through these transactions will put a stop to these things, even if there is an appeal. I think there should be an appeal; I thought that was a good suggestion, because after all one man's interpretation of a set of facts may be different from somebody else's. But as long as there is an appeal on the tax so that the general public is protected, it seems to me that the government revenue should also be protected; and this is a good way to provide that protection until such time as the people who have been asked to study this question in detail can come up with a solution, which may or may not prove to be satisfactory to hon. members.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two features about this question upon

which I would like to comment. First of all, the minister did indicate that he thought the tax should not be retroactive. I think he will agree that it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

It is, in effect, to the point that the minister may examine any transaction where a payment may be effected. It says in paragraph 16(c):
-which amount, in the opinion of the minister, was received by the taxpayer as part of a transaction or series of transactions whenever effected-
I cannot put any other connotation on that but that it predated June 13-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I just answer the hon. member's question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that in reading the words the hon. member is entitled to interpret it that way. In my explanation I pointed out -I would like to repeat the words that I used-that, moreover, in the administration of this provision it is not intended to apply to cases where the series of transactions in question commenced prior to budget night. I wanted to put that on the record and to make it clear that it is not intended to make this provision retroactive.
Yes, that is right.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to say something about the question of appeal. I was glad to hear the minister say it was a good suggestion, particularly because in this paragraph it says "in the opinion of the minister". There are two points I should like to raise with regard to a right of appeal. Supposing you do have a right of appeal? You can never really upset, on appeal, a discretion that has been properly exercised. That is difficult, unless it is spelled out in statute. I hope that goes in. There is a great deal of law on this subject. I have appeared before the appeal board and they have pointed out that if it is an administrative discretion properly exercised, it is difficult to upset. Therefore how can a taxpayer appearing before the appeal board or the exchequer court ever win an appeal before those tribunals that a discretion has been improperly exercised under paragraph 16, unless there is something in the law to this effect? The courts have never said there is anything wrong in law if somebody pays the least amount of tax possible. But I realize the minister is trying to plug the loophole and-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member will allow me to interrupt him and draw his attention to paragraph 18, which deals with this matter.

I realize that, Mr. Chairman, but I still say it is a question of law. There is nothing to prevent anybody appearing before the appeal board; but it is very difficult to prove that an administrative discretion has been improperly exercised.
There is one other matter which makes it difficult. I think we should appreciate it is really not the discretion of the minister but of someone in his department. Some bureaucrat-and I use the word with respect-says that a file will be reviewed. A year or two passes and there is a four-year limitation. What has been done is legal but actually the law has been circumvented. As the hon. member for Port Arthur said, the tax has been cut down and in effect we are legislators unto ourselves. Even though parliament has created the law, in the opinion of a bureaucrat what you have done is to cut your tax position. The amount of tax which goes to the Department of National Revenue has been cut down and a reassessment is ordered with a view to more tax being paid. Not only in this section but all through the Income Tax Act you run into this problem. You cannot upset this discretion in an appeal court or in the exchequer court, as I have tried to do on many occasions.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to anticipate the debate on section 18 with regard to the question of the opinion of the minister. This is one of the few areas in which there is a discretion under the Income Tax Act, one which I think historically we could go into at great length. After my connection of three years with the Department of National Revenue, which true enough was not as close as it might have been at times, nevertheless I have sufficient insight to know that discretion is the one thing which the minister does not want. If he has a discretion he is put under intolerable pressure. Be that as it may, no opportunity is given to those assessors to say: "Yes, you reduced your tax liability but we think you should not; therefore we are reassessing you". The minister will also readily understand that he will never appeal under section 18. The person who has a favourable ruling also will not appeal. Therefore only the taxpayer who is disappointed by a ruling or has what he considers an adverse ruling will appeal. The appeal is only to the exchequer court, not to the tax appeal board. I suggest to the hon. member that he is using a mallet to do the job of a tack hammer in many instances. Conversely there is a discouraging of appeals by forcing a taxpayer into the exchequer court. I would have preferred to do away entirely with the question of opinion. It may be administratively difficult to lay down
Income Tax Act
the four corners of the rules governing dividend stripping, but I suggest to the minister that in the long run this would be preferable. Even if some people did slip through there is always the chance of coming back next year and plugging the holes.
There is an omnibus type of regulation here which I think goes against the principle of a great deal of the Income Tax Act. We should remember that the onus will be on the taxpayer to prove that the minister exercised his discretion in the wrong way. If the minister has appeared before the courts he will know that this is almost impossible to do, because the courts will not substitute their discretion for the discretion of an administrative official or the minister, provided the discretion has been lawfully exercised. With the greatest respect to the minister and the people who drafted this provision, I do not think the question of appeal means very much, and really the objections in this regard have not been met.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to say two things. First of all, you can let this thing go, but the government have decided that there are a lot of loopholes in the act which should be plugged. This is one of the most glaring ones. It is fine to say that we should nail down the four corners; but a few minutes ago, in answer to the hon. member for Port Arthur, I said that this was a highly complex issue. Governments have been trying to nail this one down for a long time, without success. If my hon. friend doubts me I would refer him to Mr. Stikeman's dissertations, to which the hon. member for Port Arthur referred. Or if he wants to get through one of these things I might refer him to Mr. Stike-man. It is hoped that the royal commission on taxation will come up with a formula which will deal with this subject. The question is, should we leave the gate open until then, or should we try and close it in this way-because I know of no other way to do it quickly-for the time being?
As far as appeal is concerned, with the greatest respect to the hon. member for Edmonton West, I think that when we come to section 18 he will see that the appeal provisions are much wider and cover much more than just an appeal against the discretion of the minister. I do not know whether I should discuss this now or wait until we get to it, but it is really intended to cover a lot more ground than the hon. member dealt with.

Would the minister consider this question; it is a suggestion as well as a question. This can be done in the United States, I believe, but not here. If the taxpayer were able to go to the officials of the

Income Tax Act
department and say: "If I move A, B, and C in business, will this be a capital gain or something else?" it might be clear. The trouble is that it is difficult to see whether businesses are taxable because of an honest movement to better the business and to make it more efficient. That is a problem which business runs into.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Speaking personally, and only personally, I could not agree more with the hon. member. I should like to see the day when any taxpayer or businessman can go to the department and ask for a prospective ruling. I am not suggesting that at the moment because my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue would point out to me that his department is badly understaffed and simply could not handle it. Perhaps the answer to it is to give him sufficient staff to deal with these matters in the way which has been suggested, but I am afraid that cannot be done right away. It takes trained and expert staff to handle these matters, and such people cannot be picked up off the street in a week or two.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, having received an invitation on philosophical grounds twice in one evening I find it difficult to resist confessing that I was rather disturbed to find the hon. member for Port Arthur could not remember the name of the constituency which I represent. Because in better days he knew that part of Montreal which I represent pretty well. It embraces, among other parts of the city, St. Catherine Street and St. Lawrence-Main where the strip is not entirely unknown.
What about the Jacques Cartier bridge?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
No, not quite the Jacques Cartier bridge. In any event, he invited me to provide some philosophical uplift to this debate. I would agree with the minister that this is a loophole which has to be closed, but as long as it remained a loophole in the Income Tax Act the taxpayer was entitled to take advantage of it, if you will, and to exercise his common law right, as expressed by a famous Scottish judge and member of the privy council at the turn of the century, a precept which is still accepted as part of the law of this country, namely that a man is entitled to arrange his affairs so as to involve himself in the least amount of tax. So that while that loophole existed the taxpayers of this country were quite legitimately exercising their common law right to reduce the amount of tax they had to pay to the department.

On the subject introduced by the hon. member for Bow River and mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton West, I would agree that before resolution 18 was added there might have been something in what he said. Had there been no provision for appeal in the resolution, a taxpayer would have been severely limited because the courts have held that where there is no provision for appeal a taxpayer cannot bypass a minister's discretion unless it has not been rightly exercised, or it has not been exercised honestly and fairly, or the principle of natural justice has not been brought into play. As the hon. member for Edmonton West knows, this is a virtually impossible task.
Now provision for appeal has been made in resolution 18 and there is to be a review of the minister's discretionary power. It may be that the wording of resolution 18 is narrow. It says there is an appeal to the exchequer court, but the court may vacate any discretion of the minister only where none of the purposes of the transaction was to effect a surplus strip. Since every corporate transaction has a number of purposes, the company will have to prove that none of them was for that purpose and it might be difficult for a shareholder or a taxpayer to provide such proof.
While I am on my feet-I notice this is the standard ploy for retaining the attention of the house, or the committee, for a further period, may I ask the minister this: in his opening statement he said that this resolution would not apply to any transaction which came into force prior to the night of the budget. Do I understand the hon. gentleman to mean that it applies to transactions executed or consumated before the budget date? What would be the situation if shares issued as a result of one of these transactions prior to the budget date were subsequently redeemed? If they came within the provisions of this resolution the resolution would, in effect, be a retroactive one.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does that complete the discussion on paragraph 16?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I was wondering whether the minister would direct his attention to those points, then I would possibly wish to ask him another question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not particularly want to direct my attention to it. I do not think I have any more to say. This provision is not intended to be retroactive, which means it does not apply to any series of transactions which were commenced before budget night. It does mean that if there is anything more than a gleam in the girl's eye, it does apply.
How do they assess the gleam in a girl's eye?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am too old for that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I must say, in answer to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, that the courts have been inquiring into the state of a man's digestion. The gleam in a girl's eye is just another step beyond that.
This provision applies to any redemption of preferred shares as a result of any bona fide reorganization, whether or not such a reorganization arises out of what is called dividend stripping. I suggest a distinction should be made between a transaction where preferred shares are issued to clear out past surpluses, where you do have what is known as a strip, and a preferred share situation which is built up in order to meet future earnings. The latter situation is a common one and is a standard move for a parent company to take income out of a subsidiary. I submit that this type of transaction should not be caught by the motive behind the resolution.
I believe the Department of National Revenue will be faced with serious problems in dealing with legitimate cases of estate planning where a man tries to pass his business into the hands of his family by setting up a holding company and issuing preferred shares as a consideration for the value of that business. This type of completely bona fide situation might well be caught by the wide drafting of the resolution as it stands at present. I therefore respectfully say to the minister and his officials that care must be taken to draw a line between perfectly legitimate mergers or corporate reorganization plans, and the type of situation which it is sought to combat. If the ordinary estate plan is caught, if the ordinary corporate reorganization is caught, if the ordinary family business is caught, the small town counsel mentioned by the hon. member for Perth, the small business man, are among those likely to be in difficulty. They do not have available to them the more sophisticated advice which may be found in the larger cities. We should be careful in drafting to protect the average small businessman or the family man arranging his business affairs, because these are the people who have recourse only to the type of local advice described by the hon. member for Port Arthur.

I think the committee owes something to the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George for having dealt with this situation as clearly as he has. I have been advised by lawyers who are dealing with these problems every day that in view of the possible meanings of this provision they cannot
Income Tax Act
advise their clients to enter into any transaction of this kind in any circumstances unless they have had a declaration by the department that they would not be liable for tax. Some of us who have had dealings with the Department of National Revenue know how difficult it is to get a ruling in advance as to what may happen. Certainly we are dealing with a situation which is causing a great deal of concern to the learned fraternity, accountants and others. I appreciate the fact that the minister is attempting to deal with this situation and to deal with the criticism which was raised on an earlier occasion; but I wish to emphasize what has been said by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. There is a very real problem here, with respect, not to any of these huge corporations, though they might become involved, but with respect to ordinary Canadian citizens as well as citizens in the United States I am not sure when the bill is coming in, but I would hope the minister would arrange to delay its introduction until after the discussion on the resolution so that some modifications may possibly be made. I would hope that when the bill comes in there would be changes or some elasticity in the wording of it which would meet the criticism that has just been made.

I should like to return to the question I have been trying to put, probably ineffectually, to the minister. Why does the minister not consider a means of gaining some revenue for the crown, maybe on a one shot basis, from this situation where so many of these corporations are being driven to this dividend stripping process? I notice that Mr. MacKay said in 1952:
The government is therefore now facing a problem, long overdue, of finding some way to allow accumulated income on hand to be distributed without the imposition of such burdens of tax as the shareholders would be unwilling to pay.
He goes on to point out that this problem was met on a number of occasions in the past,^ in 1929, 1939 and 1949, when special provisions were made. It seems to me that this is the logic of an outsider looking at the situation. If you dam the loopholes the accumulation is likely to go on, and that is not going to attain the objective, which I assume would be in the minds of the taxation officials, of getting an opportunity to tax the revenue.
If this is the situation, then is there not some incentive that can be given to have these surpluses disbursed to the shareholders by some particular measure such as has been taken in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is provision, of course, that under certain circumstances the surplus can be withdrawn upon payment of the 15

Income Tax Act
per cent tax which people are apparently unwilling to pay. That is one of the troubles. The provision is there and it does not apply in all cases, but to a large extent this stripping is to avoid the 15 per cent tax.
I think that the hon. member's point is very well taken and I would hope that the royal commission would come up with a solution perhaps along the line suggested by the hon. member. But in the meantime what should we do? Should we leave the loophole open or should we try to plug it until we find a solution? This is one of the things that the royal commission has been asked to do since this government came into power. I have had conversations with the chairman of the royal commission and have suggested to him that this is one of the things on which we would like an early study and an early recommendation. If I had been confident that we would get a recommendation within a very short time, perhaps it would have been better to leave this, but I do not think we can be certain of that. So it seemed to me that it was better to do something to plug this loophole for the time being, although I admit this is not an appropriate permanent solution. As I expect the hon. member knows, any company that pays a dividend of say 50 per cent of its earnings can distribute the other 50 per cent on payment of a 15 per cent tax, but that is something people do not want to pay.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does this complete the discussion on paragraph 16?

No, Mr. Chairman. I am wondering whether the minister considered proposing as an alternative the charging of a flat rate, say a 15 per cent levy. Thereby those people would carry out their intentions and we would also avoid some of the pitfalls which it would seem to be indicated may be engendered by the resolution, if it is not too well drafted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That might be a rough way of dealing with this thing. It may be the proposal that the royal commission may come up with, for all I know; but in this case anyway I thought it might be better to wait until I had the advice of the royal commission, and not make a snap decision of that kind which might appeal to the hon. member for Edmonton West but perhaps might prove to have some weaknesses in it.
With the greatest respect, there was no snap decision. I would have thought that perhaps the snap decisions were those of other people, and that one should not get into those troubles.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does this complete consideration of paragraph 16? Paragraph 17.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the next paragraph, which deals with associated companies, proposes that the Minister of National Revenue be given the authority to look at the arrangements where a company or an enterprise is split up into a number of companies in order to reduce its income tax. This is another measure to plug loopholes. The need for this amendment arises because the first $35,000 of taxable income of a company is taxed at only 21 per cent compared with a rate of 50 per cent, or 52 per cent in the case of Ontario and Quebec, on taxable incomes in excess of $35,000.
Because of this differential in rates a strong incentive is provided for companies to be split into many smaller companies, each having an income of $35,000 or less. This process has been developed and engaged in by a wide variety of people. It is a loophole. If there are eight or 10 companies that are clearly associated and each one's affairs are arranged in such a way that their profits come to less than $35,000, in the aggregate they only pay a 21 per cent tax, whereas if they were merged as they normally would be they would be paying a 52 per cent tax, or a 50 per cent tax in provinces other than Ontario and Quebec. This would seem to me like a pretty big loophole and there would be a fairly good argument for doing something about it. That is the purpose of this provision.
Is not the determination of this matter made on the basis of whether oi not the companies are at arm's length?

There are two things I should like to say. First of all, I still have some objections with regard to a minister exercising his discretion in examining these companies to see whether there is in fact any association. Fundamentally, however, I have a much greater objection to the manner in which taxation is imposed so far as associated companies are concerned. This is no secret. It is not the first time I have expressed my opposition, and I think it arises fundamentally from the distinction between so-called small business and large business, with this wide difference in the level of taxation involving the two rates, 21 per cent and 50 per cent.
I think it would have been far better for the minister to take his courage in his hands and say: All right, we are going to tax at a rate of 18 per cent, 20 per cent or X per cent right across the board on all corporate profits, but then have a rather heavy rate of taxation on withdrawals in the form of dividends, and so on, together with appropriate incentives, on the other hand, to loosen up surplus accounts.

To my mind there is a case for the grouping together of associated companies. The government is simply saying these are various departments of one large business, so let us treat them all as an entity. I do not know what the situation is like in central Canada but I do know that in western Canada this type of taxation has done a great deal to deter equity investment by an individual who takes a portion of a company by associating himself with local capital and local management, and encouraging it. I know of any number of companies which went into a city or town and enlisted local capital with local management to give that incentive of local interest.
Frankly, under this provision it is becoming more and more difficult to do this because everything is deemed to be in the hands of the principal company or the principal investor. I would suggest to the minister that we are taking a retrograde step with regard to this type of taxation, and the sooner we get out of it the better off we will be. I am quite opposed to this idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask a question? Would the hon. member think it would be proper to tax all companies at the 50 per cent level? Is that what he wants?

No, not at the 50 per cent rate; I think that is strictly punitive taxation. I would have thought it would be preferable to tax them at some lower rate, and then tax the withdrawal at a much higher rate so that you leave the capital. This, I think, would be an incentive to Canadian capital to build up within the corporation. Frankly, this way we are driving available capital out of our corporate structure. It was for the purpose of allowing smaller corporations to develop and build up that we instituted this lower rate of 21 per cent. This was certainly stated to be the purpose of it. I think we are defeating that purpose now by this business of association.
I reiterate my opposition to it, and I feel that there is a discretion. I do not believe the appeal provision is satisfactory. The onus is still on the taxpayer who has an adverse ruling to take the minister to the exchequer court, and in the case of a small company this is not a light burden.

I understand that by legislation effective January, 1963, a number of companies have been deemed to be associated and some dissociated. Does the minister intend to respect the decisions that have been made concerning associated and dissociated companies?
My second question is, does the minister intend to give any consideration to the fact that some of these companies may be engaged
Income Tax Act
in different types of activities that, in effect, two companies may have very different purposes and be in very different types of business, and will that have anything to do with the decision that might be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, in answer to the hon.
member's question, the fact that companies have not been deemed to be associated in the past may have nothing to do with the fact that they are associated now.
If in the past the treasury has deemed two or three companies are not associated, and the agreements they have had have been accepted, can the minister now review them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the past an assessor had no right to say any such thing.

There were certain regulations in respect of associated companies. Certainly, scores and scores of agreements were made in legal offices throughout the country whereby you worked around your shareholdings so you did not have associated companies within the meaning of the regulations as they stood prior to June 13. Now, if those agreements have been accepted by the Department of National Revenue as not being caught by the net, are they now going to be subject to review by the minister who says: Oh yes, I think they really are and that the true intent is they are associated companies and therefore subject to tax?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question. Does he make any differentiation between a company that is splitting up its holdings into various companies and a company that is expanding by virtue of the proprietor saying that he will take out the dividends from his stock and take this money out of the company. Then, he puts this money into a new company, a completely separate entity. I think there is a vast difference between splitting up a company for the purpose of avoiding tax and a person taking his money or his profits out of a company and then putting it into a new company. He will become a major shareholder in both companies, but the intentions are vastly different because he is actually expanding the economy, whereas in the other case there is a division of companies to avoid the payment of tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think we should get back to the original intention when this lower rate of taxation was introduced. The purpose was to help the small businessman, the retailer or small processor, with relatively small profits.

Income Tax Act
I think, originally, the ceiling was set at $25,000, or it may have been $20,000. Then, a year or two ago it was changed to $35,000. The purpose was to assist the smaller businessman by providing a lower rate of taxation than was provided for the larger corporations. The purpose was to help the smaller businessman, not the man who had a lot of capital or the investor in either' one large corporation or a series of corporations.
I think the point has been made that when you have this wide differential in rate of taxation, 21 per cent as against 50 per cent, naturally that difference is an encouragement to people to try to get around it. Perhaps there is something to be said for the hon. member's suggestion that there should be a uniform rate of taxation, but it certainly is not a suggestion that would appeal to the small businessman in this country.
If it is lower than 21 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would remind hon. members it is fairly difficult to get revenues. I do not think if you levelled up the 21 per cent to a higher rate it would really mean that the 50 per cent rate could be reduced appreciably. I could find out.
You would need a terrific amount of research and statistics to ascertain that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we have the statistics. Here, we have a choice it seems to me of raising the tax for the small businesses in the country that are incorporated or, alternatively, trying to do something about people who are essentially getting around this provision. This is the purpose of this resolution.

Perhaps I am a little thick between the ears, but I do not understand this. We want to expand industry. In my proposition I am not considering the man who establishes a subsidiary company. This is one thing. I am considering an individual who has earnings from a particular company, which is separate from the corporation, and who takes his money out of that corporation. Then he pays his tax on the money he takes out, but he reinvests that money in, say, an apartment block. The question I am interested in is whether this man, if he reinvests in some other enterprise, is going to be on the same plane as a corporation that has a subsidiary? I do not think he should be, and there should be a difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the hon. member's example represents a small businessman who is no longer a small businessman. He is two

or three small businessmen. I do not think there is any perfection in this, but I suspect that this man was not the person for whom this lower rate of tax was designed. He is a graduate from that.

I thank the minister, but what I am after here is that a corporation which divides a company for the avoidance of tax is in a different position from a person who takes his savings out and establishes a new company.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Shall I rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

subtopic: STATEMENT AGREED ON 21ST JULY, 1963 BETWEEN REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES

speechtext:
Representatives of Canada and the United States met during the week end to appraise the impact on the Canadian financial markets of the proposed United States interest equalization tax.
The two governments recognized the need for effective action to improve the balance of payments position of both countries and are both equally determined that such action shall not impair the intimate economic relationships between the two countries, nor impede the growth essential for both economies.
For many years the capital markets of the two countries have been closely interconnected, and United States exports of capital to Canada have financed a substantial portion of the Canadian current account deficit with the U.S. This need continues. A portion of these flows must be supplied through the sale of new issues of Canadian securities in American markets. U.S. officials had considered that ample flows for these needs would continue under the proposed interest equalization tax. However, Canadian representatives stated that this would require a very substantial rise in the entire Canadian interest rate structure. It was recognized by both governments that such a development would be undesirable in present economic circumstances.
In the light of this situation U.S. officials agreed that the draft legislation to be submitted to the congress would include a provision
authorizing a procedure under which the President could modify the application of the tax by the establishment from time to time of exemptions, which he could make either unlimited or limited in amount. The President would thus have the flexibility to permit tax free purchases of new issues needed to maintain the unimpeded flow of trade and payments between the two countries, and to take care of exceptional situations that might arise in the case of other countries. U.S. officials made clear that this did not modify their proposals regarding the taxation of transactions in outstanding securities; over the past year such transactions between Canada and the U.S. have not been a major factor.
The Canadian authorities stated that it would not be the desire or intention of Canada to increase her foreign exchange reserves through the proceeds of borrowings in the United States, and it is the hope and expectation of both governments that by maintaining close consultation it will prove possible in practice to have an unlimited exemption for Canada without adverse effect on the United States.
It was agreed that active consultations would continue to strengthen the close economic relations between the two countries and at the same time facilitate measures for making the maximum practicable contributions to economic expansion and the strength and stability of both currencies.
Tuesday, July 23, 1963
